# Deployed status — May 28, 2026

Product Engineering deployed Lantern PR 1089's tenant-scoped published-service alias resolution for Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce on May 28, 2026.

# Resolution rule

Lantern may resolve a historical service identifier only when the tenant-scoped owner map publishes an alias record containing the old identifier, the canonical published service identifier, and an effective interval covering the source event's timestamp. Both the effective interval's start timestamp and end timestamp are inclusive, so a source event timestamp equal to either endpoint is covered.

If no such record exists, the source event timestamp is earlier than the inclusive start timestamp, or the source event timestamp is later than the inclusive end timestamp, Lantern keeps the signals separate and renders ownership as explicit unknown. The UI does not infer a rename from similar names or customer context.

# Harbor Health result

The original Harbor Health `claims-edge` event now resolves to published `claims-ingest` ownership because its source timestamp is covered by the owner map's published alias interval.

# Regression evidence

Across 28 executed fixtures:
- All 12 valid in-interval aliases joined to their canonical published service identifiers.
- Eight out-of-interval aliases remained separate with explicit unknown ownership.
- Eight identifiers with no published alias record remained separate with explicit unknown ownership.

# Affected safety rerun

Alex's affected safety rerun found no cross-tenant resolution, missing provenance, unpublished ownership render, excluded field, adapter call after denial, or loss of read-only enforcement.

# Approved customer-facing wording

Authorized join: `Published service identity resolved from an owner-map alias effective at this source event timestamp.`

No qualifying alias: `Ownership unknown: no published owner-map alias covers this source event timestamp.`

# Unchanged boundary

The deployment applies only to Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce. It adds no heuristic identity inference and does not expand the customer data contract.

## July 3, 2026 — deployed overlap correction

Lantern now evaluates every tenant-scoped owner-map alias whose inclusive effective interval covers the source event timestamp. If all qualifying records identify the same canonical published service, Lantern resolves that identity once. If qualifying records identify two or more distinct canonical services, Lantern keeps the signals separate and renders ownership as explicit unknown regardless of storage order. Both effective-interval endpoints remain inclusive.

## Scope
A bounded tabletop scoring sheet, not a production runbook. Score observable responder behavior for an accepted metrics-router action across cancellation, caller disconnect, process recovery, and publication.

- Pass: Responders identify the durable acceptance boundary and preserve one attempt identity after acceptance.
- Fail: They create, assume, or accept multiple identities for the same accepted attempt.

2. Terminal accounting
- Pass: Every accepted attempt reaches exactly one terminal result.
- Fail: An accepted attempt has no terminal result or exposes conflicting terminal results.

3. Failure classification
- Pass: Responders distinguish cancellation, caller disconnect, process recovery, and publication using the acceptance boundary.
- Fail: They collapse those cases or treat a pre-acceptance event as evidence about accepted work.

Responders must first determine whether durable acceptance occurred before interpreting cancellation, caller disconnect, process recovery, or publication. After acceptance, they must preserve one durable attempt identity and exactly one terminal result.

# Deployed status — May 28, 2026

Product Engineering deployed Lantern PR 1089's tenant-scoped published-service alias resolution for Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce on May 28, 2026.

# Resolution rule

Lantern may resolve a historical service identifier only when the tenant-scoped owner map publishes an alias record containing the old identifier, the canonical published service identifier, and an effective interval covering the source event's timestamp. Both the effective interval's start timestamp and end timestamp are inclusive, so a source event timestamp equal to either endpoint is covered.

If no such record exists, the source event timestamp is earlier than the inclusive start timestamp, or the source event timestamp is later than the inclusive end timestamp, Lantern keeps the signals separate and renders ownership as explicit unknown. The UI does not infer a rename from similar names or customer context.

# Harbor Health result

The original Harbor Health `claims-edge` event now resolves to published `claims-ingest` ownership because its source timestamp is covered by the owner map's published alias interval.

# Regression evidence

Across 28 executed fixtures:
- All 12 valid in-interval aliases joined to their canonical published service identifiers.
- Eight out-of-interval aliases remained separate with explicit unknown ownership.
- Eight identifiers with no published alias record remained separate with explicit unknown ownership.

# Affected safety rerun

Alex's affected safety rerun found no cross-tenant resolution, missing provenance, unpublished ownership render, excluded field, adapter call after denial, or loss of read-only enforcement.

# Approved customer-facing wording

Authorized join: `Published service identity resolved from an owner-map alias effective at this source event timestamp.`

No qualifying alias: `Ownership unknown: no published owner-map alias covers this source event timestamp.`

# Unchanged boundary

The deployment applies only to Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce. It adds no heuristic identity inference and does not expand the customer data contract.

## July 3, 2026 — deployed overlap correction

Lantern now evaluates every tenant-scoped owner-map alias whose inclusive effective interval covers the source event timestamp. If all qualifying records identify the same canonical published service, Lantern resolves that identity once. If qualifying records identify two or more distinct canonical services, Lantern keeps the signals separate and renders ownership as explicit unknown regardless of storage order. Both effective-interval endpoints remain inclusive.

Executed regressions show the overlapping Harbor Health `claims-ingest` and `claims-router` records failing closed in both row orders, both inclusive endpoints working, and a single valid match resolving normally. Alex's affected safety rerun found no cross-tenant resolution, missing provenance, unpublished ownership render, excluded field, adapter call after denial, or loss of read-only enforcement.

The correction is live for Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce. Their two-account read-only scope and customer data contract remain unchanged.

# Q4 incident practice — November 18 scoring sheet

## Scope
A bounded tabletop scoring sheet, not a production runbook. Score observable responder behavior for an accepted metrics-router action across cancellation, caller disconnect, process recovery, and publication.

## Core criteria
1. Durable attempt identity
- Pass: Responders identify the durable acceptance boundary and preserve one attempt identity after acceptance.
- Fail: They create, assume, or accept multiple identities for the same accepted attempt.

2. Terminal accounting
- Pass: Every accepted attempt reaches exactly one terminal result.
- Fail: An accepted attempt has no terminal result or exposes conflicting terminal results.

3. Failure classification
- Pass: Responders distinguish cancellation, caller disconnect, process recovery, and publication using the acceptance boundary.
- Fail: They collapse those cases or treat a pre-acceptance event as evidence about accepted work.

## Wes — responder path
Responders must first determine whether durable acceptance occurred before interpreting cancellation, caller disconnect, process recovery, or publication. After acceptance, they must preserve one durable attempt identity and exactly one terminal result.

## Nadia — postmortem criteria
The postmortem must name the absent system guarantee or control. It must not treat the triggering operator action as the root cause, and it must retain the mapped implementation and rollback owner.

## Final ownership-boundary condition
- Pass: Mapped owners retain implementation and rollback decisions, while the triggered reviewer remains confined to the named failure-mode boundary.
- Fail: The triggered review is treated as implementation, release, or rollback approval.

## Additional operating checks — November 8

### 45-minute secondary boundary
- Pass: When the cause remains unisolated, responders engage the secondary before the 45-minute boundary and make the incident clock visible.
- Fail: Responders wait until or after 45 minutes, or continue without engaging the secondary while the cause remains unisolated.

### Friday staging preparation versus production change
- Pass: Responders identify staging preparation that makes no production state change as staging work and separately identify a Friday-afternoon production deploy as prohibited.
- Fail: Responders classify staging-only preparation as a production deploy, or permit a Friday-afternoon production state change because it was described as preparation.

These checks supplement the accepted cancellation, caller-disconnect, durable-attempt, terminal-result, mapped-owner, and postmortem criteria. This remains a tabletop scoring sheet rather than a production runbook.

## November 18 execution order

- 5 minutes: role and ownership framing.
- 35 minutes: cancellation and caller-disconnect scenario.
- 10 minutes: one targeted rerun if a scoring boundary is missed.
- 10 minutes: debrief and owner follow-up.

Wes teaches the responder path. Nadia owns the postmortem section. Alex maintains only the bounded failure case. This is the exact one-hour tabletop sequence and does not turn the scoring sheet into a production runbook.

## Observed results — November 18

The tabletop is complete. Responders correctly separated durable acceptance from cancellation, caller disconnect, and process recovery; preserved one attempt identity and one terminal result in the exercise; identified Wes as the mapped metrics-router implementation, release, and rollback owner; and distinguished Friday staging preparation from a production change.

The first run engaged the secondary at minute 47 while the cause remained unisolated, missing the required before-45-minute boundary. The targeted rerun engaged the secondary at minute 42 and passed that boundary. Nadia’s debrief named the missing system control rather than the triggering operator action as root cause.

These results are training evidence only. The tabletop did not execute the product implementation and does not close any product defect or replace required executable product evidence.

The first 16.0-million-points/minute Mosaic-shaped replay exposed the initial constraint: queue-wait p99 reached 780 ms and retryable queue-full responses reached 0.9%, exceeding the bounded-control thresholds. Accepted batches remained intact, while shard-keeper lease health and rollup-service parity stayed at baseline—isolating the shared metrics-router export queue rather than a cross-service consistency defect.

The later 19.78-million-points/minute staged replay, using the updated forecast mix, qualified cleanly: queue-wait p99 was 319 ms, retryable queue-full responses were 0.17%, and the highest tenant reached 62 pending batches. Every accepted batch reconciled to exactly one terminal result with no loss; consistency, parity, dropped-series, route, shard-keeper lease, rollup-service, and full-health checks remained at baseline, with no cross-service invariant or failure-mode exception.

Capacity conclusion: the first replay established that the original 16.0M load was beyond the initial queue margin but did not reveal downstream corruption; the later replay established qualified staged capacity at 19.78M under the bounded control. No—the later replay supplied staged evidence only and did not authorize a production window or production change.

arguments.title: Lantern final review decision record — October 8, 2025
arguments.body:
Lantern final review decision record

Decision date: October 8, 2025
Reviewers/authorizers: Hema and Theo
Evidence window: July 1–September 18, 2025
Authorized accounts: Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce only

Decision
Hema and Theo authorize Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce, and no other accounts, to continue uninterrupted with read-only access from October 11, 2025 through March 31, 2026. This decision records continuation of the existing bounded two-account preview; it does not authorize broader adoption or determine any later Lantern platform direction.

Reconciled evidence
The July 1–September 18 evidence is preserved as reconciled:
• 2,412 customer sessions.
• 463 logical explanation requests.
• 307 eligible combined explanations.
• 103 valid over-24-hour cases, kept separate.
• 53 explicit-unknown outcomes.
• 0 eligible renderer failures.
• No automatic-stop condition identified.
• 1,842 post-correction deploy-card rows, with no delivery retry rendered as a duplicate deploy movement.

The technical evidence above remains separate from customer feedback. It is evidence for this bounded decision and is not a release-readiness source of truth.

Customer feedback (separate from technical evidence)
• Harbor Health used the corrected systems view in four release follow-ups and requested continuation.
• Mosaic Commerce used the corrected systems view in three incident handoffs and requested continuation.
These observations are customer feedback only and do not expand the authorized scope.

Existing two-account contract and data boundary
Access remains read-only and limited to:
• provenance-backed deploy movement;
• published service ownership;
• timestamped incident-load summaries; and
• explicit unknown states.

No additional account, cost data, CSV export, raw incident text, internal room metadata, employee identifier or comparison, inferred or unpublished ownership, internal-only fallback data, or write capability is authorized. The owner map is unchanged.

Monitoring ownership
• Alex owns freshness, tenant-isolation, authorization-denial, latency, error, and failure-mode monitoring.
• Iris owns customer interpretation and feedback.
This monitoring split is unchanged.

Immediate suspension conditions
Both Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce must be suspended immediately, pending correction and a successful rerun of the affected safety check, if any of the following occurs:
• an authorization-wrapper bypass;
• an adapter call after denial;
• cross-tenant material;
• a stale or missing source rendered as anything other than explicit unknown;
• a deploy event without required provenance;
• unpublished ownership;
• an incident-load summary without its source timestamp;
• exposure of any excluded field; or
• loss of read-only enforcement.

Latency and other errors do not independently suspend the preview unless they cause one of the violations above.

Non-decisions and boundary
This decision authorizes neither broader adoption nor any later Lantern platform direction. It adds no accounts, data categories, cost context, export capability, raw incident access, internal metadata, employee comparison, inferred ownership, unpublished ownership, fallback data, or write capability. Customer requests for continuation do not alter those boundaries.

arguments.title: Lantern April 1–June 15 operating-evidence review prep
arguments.body:
Lantern April 1–June 15 operating-evidence review prep

Review
- Review: Lantern post-transition operating-evidence review
- Date/time: June 24, 2026, 10:30–11:15 AM Eastern
- Participants: Alex Valdez, Iris, Hema, Product Engineering
- Evidence window: April 1 through June 15, 2026, inclusive
- Purpose: Prepare and reconcile the frozen operating evidence for review. This document is preparation material, not a customer-use conclusion, scope authorization, recommendation, or statement of the June 24 result.

Boundary and permitted surface
- Authorized accounts: Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce only. Preserve the two-account, read-only boundary.
- Permitted surface only: provenance-backed deploy movement; published service ownership; timestamped incident-load summaries; and explicit unknown states when permitted input is stale, missing, malformed, unavailable, or not permissioned.
- No additional account, cost data, CSV export, raw incident text, internal room metadata, employee identifier or comparison, inferred or unpublished ownership, internal-only fallback data, readiness judgment, or write capability.
- Evidence must not presume customer use or imply that evidence alone authorizes new scope.

Roles and inputs
- Product Engineering: supply the frozen April 1–June 15 operating export, including the raw denominators and safety traces needed for reconciliation.
- Alex: reconcile customer sessions; logical explanation categories; provenance and permission checks; and automatic-stop conditions.
- Iris: provide customer-use interpretation separately from the technical evidence. Do not turn interpretation into a technical control result, readiness judgment, causal claim, or scope decision.
- Hema: chair the review and keep evidence, interpretation, and decisions distinct.

Evidence reconciliation checklist
[ ] Confirm the export is frozen for the inclusive April 1–June 15 window and is limited to Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce.
[ ] Reconcile total customer sessions to the export's session denominator; record the total and any discrepancy.
[ ] Reconcile total logical explanation requests to the categorized request records.
[ ] Reconcile eligible combined explanations: same authorized customer tenant, same published service identifier, provenance-backed permitted signals, independently valid freshness, and timestamp spread no more than 24 hours.
[ ] Reconcile valid cases kept separate because source timestamps differ by more than 24 hours; retain their source timestamps and do not describe them as contemporaneous or causally connected.
[ ] Reconcile explicit-unknown outcomes for stale or missing input (including malformed, unavailable, or not-permissioned permitted input); confirm no combined explanation was emitted for those cases.
[ ] Record eligible renderer failures separately from the explanation categories; do not silently fold failures into explicit unknowns or successful results.
[ ] Check that the category totals reconcile to the logical-request total, with any non-category or duplicate records identified and resolved before the review.
[ ] Report customer sessions, logical requests, eligible combined explanations, valid >24-hour separations, explicit-unknown outcomes, and eligible renderer failures as distinct counts. Do not infer customer use from these counts.

Technical safety checklist
Shared authorization wrapper and shared-registration path
[ ] Verify every Lantern entry point uses the same shared authorization wrapper and shared registration, with no alternate or fallback registration path.
[ ] Verify authorization completes before any source adapter is constructed or called, protected cache is read, or fallback path is evaluated.
[ ] Verify denied, missing, malformed, or failed authorization returns 403 not_authorized before source access, reveals no protected values, and has adapter_calls=0.
[ ] Verify no adapter call occurs after denial and no fallback bypasses the wrapper.
[ ] Verify authorized access remains limited to Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce and remains read-only.

Tenant, permission, provenance, and source checks
[ ] Verify tenant isolation: no cross-tenant material, joins, cache reads, or rendered values.
[ ] Verify each deploy event has required provenance and a source timestamp.
[ ] Verify each ownership result is published owner-map ownership only; no inferred, unpublished, manually patched, or internal-only ownership.
[ ] Verify each incident-load summary carries its source timestamp and passes independent permission and freshness checks.
[ ] Verify stale, missing, malformed, unavailable, or not-permissioned input renders explicit unknown, with no value timestamp presented for an absent permitted source and with a separate observation-attempt timestamp where the contract requires it.
[ ] Verify excluded-field protection: no raw incident text, internal room metadata, employee identifier or comparison, cost data, readiness label, or other excluded field appears in external fields.
[ ] Verify read-only enforcement: no write, mutation, export, or capability that expands the permitted surface.

Existing automatic-stop conditions
Suspend both accounts immediately, preserve the evidence, and require correction plus a successful rerun of the affected safety check for any of the following:
- shared authorization-wrapper bypass;
- authorization not completed before source access;
- adapter call after denial;
- cross-tenant material;
- stale or missing source rendered as anything other than explicit unknown;
- deploy event without required provenance or source timestamp;
- unpublished, inferred, or otherwise unauthorized ownership;
- incident-load summary without its source timestamp;
- exposure of an excluded field, including raw incident text, internal room metadata, employee identifiers/comparisons, cost data, or internal-only fallback data; or
- loss of read-only enforcement.
Latency and other errors do not independently suspend access unless they cause one of these violations.

Separate path verification
1. Shared-registration path
[ ] Exercise representative allowed and denied requests through each Lantern entry point.
[ ] Confirm one shared wrapper identity and identical pre-access ordering across registration paths.
[ ] Confirm allowed requests reach only the permitted read-only sources after an explicit allow.
[ ] Confirm denied requests terminate before adapter construction/source access, return 403 not_authorized, and show adapter_calls=0.
[ ] Confirm the traces demonstrate tenant isolation, excluded-field protection, explicit-unknown behavior, and no write capability.

2. Published-alias path
[ ] Verify alias effectiveness uses inclusive start and end timestamps: an alias is effective at its recorded source event timestamp when that timestamp falls on either boundary or within the interval.
[ ] Verify the Harbor Health result: source alias claims-edge resolves to the published service claims-ingest when the alias covers that source event timestamp.
[ ] Verify the approved join text is exactly: “Published service identity resolved from an owner-map alias effective at this source event timestamp.”
[ ] Verify an absent alias or an alias outside its effective interval renders explicit unknown rather than a published service identity.
[ ] Verify the approved fallback text is exactly: “Ownership unknown: no published owner-map alias covers this source event timestamp.”
[ ] Verify no heuristic rename inference, string similarity, manual override, or unpublished ownership is used when the alias is absent or out of interval.
[ ] Verify alias resolution remains tenant-scoped, provenance-backed, permission-checked, and read-only; retain the source event timestamp and relevant provenance in the evidence.

Review packet and discussion order
1. Product Engineering supplies the frozen export and technical traces.
2. Alex presents denominator/category reconciliation and safety-check results, including any automatic-stop trigger.
3. Alex presents the shared-registration and published-alias path checks separately.
4. Iris presents customer-use interpretation as a separate section, without presuming use or adding technical evidence.
5. Hema chairs questions and records only decisions actually made during the June 24 review.

Guardrails for the record
- Keep the April 1–June 15 evidence separate from older evidence cycles; do not modify or merge an older preparation or evidence document.
- Do not state the June 24 outcome early.
- Do not convert the review packet into a recommendation, customer-use claim, new authorization, broader rollout, or expanded data scope.
- If any required evidence is missing, mark it pending rather than filling the gap with inference.

arguments.title: Alex 2026 self-review — evidence draft
arguments.body:
Alex 2026 self-review — evidence draft

Status: Working draft for revision before Sphere’s Friday, November 13, 2026, 5:00 PM Eastern deadline.

Scope framing

In 2026, my impact was as an individual contributor operating across service boundaries: I defined shared technical invariants, made failure modes and authority seams explicit, and established review and escalation conditions that let mapped owners keep routine implementation, release, rollback, and operational responsibility. This draft intentionally does not claim people management, ownership of every release, or a centralized approval-gate role.

Cross-service invariants and failure modes

- Defined and reviewed invariants spanning the metrics pipeline, Lantern, and Cardinality Guardrails, with attention to provenance, authoritative source timestamps, tenant and customer-path isolation, authority duplication or mutation, label-cardinality behavior, alert-source classification, and executable parity.
- Defined Cardinality Guardrails and its authority boundaries as a first-cut, bounded contract: authority references identify authoritative records through authority_type, authority_record_id, and source_timestamp; references are read-only; authority payload values and mutation actions are not smuggled into downstream surfaces.
- Kept ownership and authority separate across the system. Lantern can reference or navigate to authoritative detail, but does not copy Cardinality Guardrails limits or cost semantics into a Lantern-owned payload or create a second authority or owner-map mutation path.
- Used explicit failure modes and exception routes rather than informal approval: missing provenance fails closed or points back to the owner-map source; mismatched authority references cannot be treated as valid; customer-path isolation remains a hard boundary; named cross-system exceptions are the trigger for my review.
- The October 22, 2026 Q4 exception-routing and owner-boundary review examined operating evidence for this model: routine Lantern work through mapped reviewers, routine metrics-router decisions remaining with Wes, and the incident-practice split between responder paths, postmortem material, and cross-service failure cases. The review was framed around preserving the existing owner model, not changing ownership or creating a centralized gate.

Technical outcomes

- Metrics-router ownership transitioned to the mapped owner model: Wes became the primary service owner and I became backup. In 2026, that boundary held for routine work rather than pulling ordinary implementation or release decisions back to me.
- On October 15, Wes handled a routine metrics-router staging route-cache parameter experiment as formal service owner, kept it in staging pending ordinary owner-run evidence, and routed implementation and release checks through mapped metrics-router reviewers without asking me for approval. The experiment did not touch tenant isolation, provenance, authoritative source timestamps, authority duplication or mutation behavior, customer-path isolation, or another named cross-system exception; it did not open a production window or change ownership.
- Corrected Lantern review routing supported the intended owner model: routine Product Engineering copy adjustment and fixture-naming cleanup proceeded through mapped reviewers without requiring my involvement. The correction addressed routing and provenance at the appropriate owner boundary rather than making me the general implementation or release gate.
- Preserved the Lantern authority boundary during the internal platform-cycle work: the reference model leaves published responsibility in the owner map, while pipeline limits and cost semantics remain in Cardinality Guardrails. Product Engineering retains implementation; Cyrus retains the Cardinality Guardrails authority interface and cost semantics; Wes retains metrics-router operating-limit mapping; Iris retains interpretation and adoption criteria; my lane is the shared cross-system contract and failure-mode review.
- Converted technical decisions into reusable guardrails, admission criteria, and exception-routing language so that routine work could proceed with less ambiguity while unsafe combinations, missing provenance, or authority mutation remained visible and reviewable.

Owner leverage

- Made the owner map and escalation paths legible enough for engineers to act through their normal review paths instead of waiting for me as a catch-all approver.
- Supported a healthier operating model in which mapped owners retain implementation, telemetry, operational-readiness, release, rollback, and responder-path decisions, while I focus on cross-service invariants and named failure-mode triggers.
- The metrics-router transition is concrete leverage: Wes could make the routine staging decision, hold it for ordinary evidence, and use mapped reviewers without returning the decision to me.
- The corrected Lantern routing is concrete leverage: Product Engineering could complete routine copy and fixture work through its mapped reviewers without requiring my review, while provenance and authority boundaries remained intact.
- The October 22 owner-boundary review provided a structured check that these boundaries were working in practice, including the split where Wes maintains responder paths, Nadia retains postmortem material, and I maintain only cross-service failure cases.
- My work on Cardinality Guardrails made cross-service risks actionable without centralizing execution: teams can check label-cardinality and alert-source conditions, preserve executable parity, and route exceptions to named owners rather than treating me as the owner of all telemetry or releases.

Boundaries that kept routine implementation with mapped owners

- I did not manage people, assign staffing, or claim people-manager responsibilities.
- I did not own every release, implementation path, rollback, or operational decision across the participating services.
- I did not become a centralized approval gate. Mapped teams remained accountable for implementation, release, rollback, and operations; my review was triggered by named cross-service invariants, failure modes, provenance concerns, authority-boundary violations, or explicit exception routes.
- I did not authorize a production window merely by reviewing a boundary, and I did not treat Lantern review activity as internal-shadow approval, customer authorization, renewal, expansion, or broader adoption.
- I did not make Lantern a second authority for owner-map, pipeline-limit, or Cardinality Guardrails data. References remained read-only and preserved the authoritative source and timestamp.
- I did not replace the service owners’ routine review paths. The evidence above shows the desired result: mapped owners made ordinary decisions, while I supplied durable contracts and cross-system escalation clarity.

Calibration summary

The evidence supports an IC scope centered on cross-service technical leadership: defining invariants, reviewing failure modes, preserving authority and provenance boundaries, and creating leverage through explicit owner handoffs and exception routes. It does not imply that I managed people, became the owner of every release, or held a centralized approval role; those responsibilities remained with mapped teams unless separately assigned.

Revision — November 9, 2026 (after narrative feedback)

This revision adds the requested quantified evidence while preserving the longer unfinished narrative above. It does not treat any November 12 review as completed or assume an outcome from it. Final verification and submission remain pending.

Updated evidence additions

1. Owner-led leverage: metrics-router

On January 20, Wes operated the metrics-router owner-led path at 17.2 million data points per minute. He made the ordinary service-owner decision without me taking over the operation or acting as an approval bottleneck. The result is evidence of leverage through a mapped owner and reusable operating boundaries: routine execution and judgment stayed with Wes, while my role remained limited to the named exception path. This is not a people-management or centralized-gate claim; it is evidence that the ownership model allowed the actual service owner to operate independently within the established boundaries.

2. Reconciled Lantern operating evidence

The reconciled June 16–September 15 Lantern evidence covers 2,476 customer sessions and 478 logical explanation requests: 319 eligible combined explanations, 104 valid cases kept separate because source timestamps differed by more than 24 hours, and 55 explicit-unknown outcomes for stale or missing input. There were zero eligible renderer failures and no listed safety violation. The audit found no authorization-wrapper bypass, adapter call after denial, cross-tenant material, stale or missing source rendered as anything other than explicit unknown, missing required provenance or source timestamp, unpublished ownership render, excluded-field exposure, or loss of read-only enforcement.

Alex 2026 self-review — evidence draft

Status: Working draft for final portal verification and submission on Friday, November 13, 2026, by 5:00 PM Eastern. The November 12 Lantern review result is incorporated; final verification and submission remain pending for tomorrow.

Scope framing

In 2026, my impact was as an individual contributor operating across service boundaries: I defined shared technical invariants, made failure modes and authority seams explicit, and established review and escalation conditions that let mapped owners keep routine implementation, release, rollback, and operational responsibility. This draft does not claim people management, ownership of every release, or a centralized approval-gate role.

Cross-service invariants and failure modes

- Defined and reviewed invariants spanning the metrics pipeline, Lantern, and Cardinality Guardrails, with attention to provenance, authoritative source timestamps, tenant and customer-path isolation, authority duplication or mutation, label-cardinality behavior, alert-source classification, and executable parity.
- Defined Cardinality Guardrails and its authority boundaries as a bounded contract: authority references identify authoritative records through authority_type, authority_record_id, and source_timestamp; references are read-only; authority payload values and mutation actions are not smuggled into downstream surfaces.
- Kept ownership and authority separate across the system. Lantern can reference or navigate to authoritative detail, but does not copy Cardinality Guardrails limits or cost semantics into a Lantern-owned payload or create a second authority or owner-map mutation path.
- Used explicit failure modes and exception routes rather than informal approval: missing provenance fails closed or points back to the owner-map source; mismatched authority references cannot be treated as valid; customer-path isolation remains a hard boundary; named cross-system exceptions are the trigger for my review.
- The October 22, 2026 Q4 exception-routing and owner-boundary review examined operating evidence for this model: routine Lantern work through mapped reviewers, routine metrics-router decisions remaining with Wes, and the incident-practice split between responder paths, postmortem material, and cross-service failure cases. The review preserved the existing owner model rather than creating a centralized gate.

Technical outcomes

- Metrics-router ownership transitioned to the mapped owner model: Wes became the primary service owner and I became backup. That boundary held for routine work rather than pulling ordinary implementation or release decisions back to me.
- On January 20, Wes operated the metrics-router owner-led path at 17.2 million data points per minute. He made the ordinary service-owner decision without me taking over the operation or acting as an approval bottleneck. Routine execution and judgment stayed with Wes; my role remained limited to the named exception path.

- Made the owner map and escalation paths legible enough for engineers to act through normal review paths instead of waiting for me as a catch-all approver.
- Supported an operating model in which mapped owners retain implementation, telemetry, operational-readiness, release, rollback, and responder-path decisions, while I focus on cross-service invariants and named failure-mode triggers.
- The metrics-router transition is concrete leverage: Wes made the January 20 routine operating decision at 17.2 million data points per minute without returning the decision to me.
- The corrected Lantern result is also bounded leverage: Product Engineering implemented and exercised the corrected staff-only build through its own path, while the contract review established the failure boundaries and the customer-path isolation requirement.
- The October 22 owner-boundary review provided a structured check that these boundaries were working in practice, including the split where Wes maintains responder paths, Nadia retains postmortem material, and I maintain only cross-service failure cases.
- My work on Cardinality Guardrails made cross-service risks actionable without centralizing execution: teams can check label-cardinality and alert-source conditions, preserve executable parity, and route exceptions to named owners rather than treating me as the owner of all telemetry or releases.

Boundaries that kept routine implementation with mapped owners

- I did not manage people, assign staffing, or claim people-manager responsibilities.
- I did not own every release, implementation path, rollback, or operational decision across the participating services.
- I did not become a centralized approval gate. Mapped teams remained accountable for implementation, release, rollback, and operations; my review was triggered by named cross-service invariants, failure modes, provenance concerns, authority-boundary violations, or explicit exception routes.

The evidence supports an IC scope centered on cross-service technical leadership: defining invariants, reviewing failure modes, preserving authority and provenance boundaries, and creating leverage through explicit owner handoffs and exception routes. Lantern reference-only internal-use decision review — December 17 final decision record

Review

December 17, 2026. Hema and Theo completed the review and approved the corrected reference-only integration for continuing internal operating use by Infra and Product Engineering, effective today.

Decision and scope

- The approval is limited to continuing internal operating use by Infra and Product Engineering.
- Internal cards may navigate staff to authoritative owner-map and Cardinality Guardrails records.
- The reference contract is limited to these fields: `tenant_id`, `canonical_service_id`, `authority_type`, `authority_record_id`, and `source_timestamp`.
- Each reference retains its own authority type, authority record ID, and source timestamp. Separate owner-map and Cardinality Guardrails references remain separate, including when attached to the same canonical service.
- Cards may not copy authority payload values, including limits or cost semantics, and may not offer mutation, write, or authority-transfer capability.
- This approval does not authorize customer exposure, customer-facing output, or a rollout into Harbor Health or Mosaic Commerce. The integration remains absent from both customer paths unless separately authorized later.

Authority boundaries

- Lantern owns explanation and navigation only; it is not an authority for owner-map values, pipeline limits, cost semantics, or published responsibility.
- Cardinality Guardrails owns pipeline limits and cost semantics.
- The owner map owns published responsibility.
- Stale or missing authority records remain explicit unknowns; Lantern must not infer, substitute, or copy authoritative values.
- The customer-path boundary remains deny-by-default and auditable. No request, artifact, output, or mutation capability may enter Harbor Health or Mosaic Commerce under this decision.

Q1 2027 operating model

Q1 2027 will proceed as three linked workstreams rather than one Lantern monolith:

1. Lantern — explanation and navigation.
2. Cardinality Guardrails — pipeline limits and cost semantics.
3. Owner map — published responsibility.

The workstreams remain linked through the shared reference contract and explicit failure boundaries; the authority boundaries above remain unchanged.

Review and implementation responsibility

Alex remains the shared-contract and failure-boundary reviewer for changes affecting tenant isolation, provenance or authoritative source timestamps, authority duplication or mutation behavior, and customer-path isolation. Alex is not the sole implementation gate. Routine implementation, review, and mapped ownership follow the applicable workstream boundaries and repository routing.

Evidence basis

The completed November 13–25 internal shadow remains the evidence basis for the decision:

- 68 staff-only reference-card renders.
- 24 dual-reference cards containing both an owner-map reference and a Cardinality Guardrails reference; all preserved separate authority record IDs and their own source timestamps.

- Iris’s interpretation check found no wording presenting either link as a Lantern-owned value, write control, or transfer of authority.
- The final customer-path audit found no request, artifact, or output in Harbor Health or Mosaic Commerce.

Recorded outcome

Continuing internal operating use is approved within the scope and contract above, effective December 17, 2026. The approval is reference-only and internal; it does not transfer authority, enable mutation, authorize customer use, or change the separate ownership of authoritative records. Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce remain unchanged and outside scope unless separately authorized later.

arguments.title: Lantern platform boundary decision record — March 26 strategy review
arguments.body:
# Lantern platform boundary decision record — March 26 strategy review

Decision date: March 26, 2026
Effective date: April 1, 2026

## Decision

After reviewing the frozen operating evidence and the divergent Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce requests, Hema and Theo decided that Lantern will become a Sphere product-platform line effective April 1, 2026, rather than remain only a narrow add-on.

The existing authorization and operating terms remain unchanged through March 31, 2026. Nothing in this decision retroactively changes the prior operating period.

## Frozen operating evidence reviewed

The frozen January 1–March 15, 2026 continuation export for the two authorized accounts recorded:

- 2,236 customer sessions.
- 431 logical explanation requests.
- 287 eligible combined explanations.
- 94 valid cases kept separate because the source timestamps differed by more than 24 hours.
- 50 explicit-unknown outcomes for stale or missing input.
- Zero eligible renderer failures.

The categories reconcile completely: 287 + 94 + 50 = 431 requests.

The safety audit found zero authorization-wrapper bypasses; adapter calls after denial; cross-tenant material; stale or missing sources rendered as anything other than explicit unknown; excluded-field exposures; deploy events missing required provenance; unpublished ownership renders; incident-load summaries missing their source timestamps; read-only enforcement losses; or other automatic-stop conditions.

Harbor Health used the existing view in seven release follow-ups. Mosaic Commerce used it in six incident handoffs.

## Boundary and responsibility split effective April 1

- Iris owns the customer promise, adoption criteria, and UI interpretation.
- Alex retains freshness, tenant-isolation, authorization-denial, latency, and error monitoring, plus the shared data contract, source-registration safety gates, and failure-mode review.
- Product Engineering owns implementation.
- Lantern explains provenance-backed service and system state.
- Cardinality Guardrails owns pipeline limits and cost signals.
- The owner map remains the source of published responsibility.

Lantern will not produce release-readiness judgments or employee-performance interpretations.

Any new source type must enter through shared registration with tenant-scoped authorization before source access, required provenance and source timestamps, explicit unknown for stale or missing input, excluded-field checks, and a successful safety rerun before customer use.

## Authorized customer access effective April 1 through September 30

Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce—and no other accounts—are authorized for continued read-only access through September 30, 2026, through the shared authorization wrapper. Access is limited to:

- Provenance-backed deploy movement.
- Published service ownership.
- Timestamped incident-load summaries.
- Explicit unknown states.

The following remain unauthorized: any additional account; cost data; CSV export; raw incident text; internal room metadata; employee identifiers or comparisons; inferred or unpublished ownership; internal-only fallback data; and any write capability.

## Immediate suspension conditions

An authorization-wrapper bypass; an adapter call after denial; cross-tenant material; stale or missing source rendered as anything other than explicit unknown; a deploy event without required provenance; unpublished ownership; an incident-load summary without its source timestamp; exposure of any excluded field; or loss of read-only enforcement immediately suspends both accounts pending correction and a successful rerun of the affected safety check.

Latency and other errors do not independently suspend access unless they cause one of those violations.

## Disposition of the divergent requests

Harbor Health’s release-readiness-label request and Mosaic Commerce’s per-service-cost request were reviewed as divergent product requests. Neither is authorized by this decision: Lantern does not produce release-readiness judgments, and Cardinality Guardrails—not Lantern—is the source for pipeline limits and cost signals.

## Record status

This document is the final decision record for the March 26 strategy review. The direction, role split, and access terms above are dated to April 1, 2026; the prior authorization and operating terms remain in force without change through March 31, 2026.

## Transition decision — recorded March 26, 2026; effective April 1, 2026

After reviewing the frozen operating evidence and the divergent Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce requests, Hema and Theo decided that Lantern will become a Sphere product-platform line effective April 1, 2026, rather than remain only a narrow add-on.

The authorization and operating terms recorded for the period through March 31, 2026 remain unchanged through that date. The new direction, role split, and access terms below are effective April 1, 2026.

Effective April 1, Iris owns the customer promise, adoption criteria, and UI interpretation. Alex retains freshness, tenant-isolation, authorization-denial, latency, and error monitoring plus the shared data contract, source-registration safety gates, and failure-mode review. Product Engineering owns implementation. Lantern explains provenance-backed service and system state, Cardinality Guardrails owns pipeline limits and cost signals, and the owner map remains the source of published responsibility.

Lantern will not produce release-readiness judgments or employee-performance interpretations. Any new source type must enter through shared registration with tenant-scoped authorization before source access, required provenance and source timestamps, explicit unknown for stale or missing input, excluded-field checks, and a successful safety rerun before customer use.

From April 1 through September 30, 2026, Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce—and no other accounts—are authorized for continued read-only access through the shared authorization wrapper. Access is limited to provenance-backed deploy movement, published service ownership, timestamped incident-load summaries, and explicit unknown states. No additional account, cost data, CSV export, raw incident text, internal room metadata, employee identifier or comparison, inferred or unpublished ownership, internal-only fallback data, or write capability is authorized.

An authorization-wrapper bypass, adapter call after denial, cross-tenant material, stale or missing source rendered as anything other than explicit unknown, deploy event without required provenance, unpublished ownership, incident-load summary without its source timestamp, exposure of any excluded field, or loss of read-only enforcement immediately suspends both accounts pending correction and a successful rerun of the affected safety check. Latency and other errors do not independently suspend access unless they cause one of those violations.

The frozen operating evidence reviewed for this transition remains the January 1–March 15, 2026 continuation export: 2,236 customer sessions; 431 logical explanation requests; 287 eligible combined explanations; 94 valid cases kept separate because source timestamps differed by more than 24 hours; 50 explicit-unknown outcomes for stale or missing input; zero eligible renderer failures; and zero audited authorization, denial-ordering, tenant-isolation, provenance, ownership, timestamp, excluded-field, read-only, or other automatic-stop violations. Harbor Health used the existing view in seven release follow-ups, and Mosaic Commerce used it in six incident handoffs. The categories reconcile to all 431 requests.

arguments.body:
Alex 2026 self-review — evidence draft

Status: Working draft for revision before Sphere’s Friday, November 13, 2026, 5:00 PM Eastern deadline.

Scope framing

In 2026, my impact was as an individual contributor operating across service boundaries: I defined shared technical invariants, made failure modes and authority seams explicit, and established review and escalation conditions that let mapped owners keep routine implementation, release, rollback, and operational responsibility. This draft intentionally does not claim people management, ownership of every release, or a centralized approval-gate role.

Cross-service invariants and failure modes

- Defined and reviewed invariants spanning the metrics pipeline, Lantern, and Cardinality Guardrails, with attention to provenance, authoritative source timestamps, tenant and customer-path isolation, authority duplication or mutation, label-cardinality behavior, alert-source classification, and executable parity.
- Defined Cardinality Guardrails and its authority boundaries as a first-cut, bounded contract: authority references identify authoritative records through authority_type, authority_record_id, and source_timestamp; references are read-only; authority payload values and mutation actions are not smuggled into downstream surfaces.
- Kept ownership and authority separate across the system. Lantern can reference or navigate to authoritative detail, but does not copy Cardinality Guardrails limits or cost semantics into a Lantern-owned payload or create a second authority or owner-map mutation path.
- Used explicit failure modes and exception routes rather than informal approval: missing provenance fails closed or points back to the owner-map source; mismatched authority references cannot be treated as valid; customer-path isolation remains a hard boundary; named cross-system exceptions are the trigger for my review.
- The October 22, 2026 Q4 exception-routing and owner-boundary review examined operating evidence for this model: routine Lantern work through mapped reviewers, routine metrics-router decisions remaining with Wes, and the incident-practice split between responder paths, postmortem material, and cross-service failure cases. The review was framed around preserving the existing owner model, not changing ownership or creating a centralized gate.

Technical outcomes

Agreed. I’d make the technical-lessons section this literal:

Technical lessons

1. Shard-keeper rollback path: The rollback was easy to make worse under pressure. It looked reversible on paper, but once state had partially moved, it was not a safe or clearly bounded operation.

2. Downstream ownership: rollup-service was effectively unowned in practice. Everyone had part of the downstream map, but nobody owned the complete consumer path.

3. Label-name diff: The label-name change needs to be explicit. Symptom alerts did not identify it; the pages looked like generic ingest weirdness rather than one label changing while a downstream consumer did not receive the change.

bookend_start.content: [2023-05-03T15:00:00-04:00] on the technical-lessons section for the Apr 18 outage, i think the cleanest shape is just name the three things and be pretty literal. `shard-keeper rollback path` was way too easy to make worse under pressure -- looked reversible on paper, wasn't once state had partially moved. then the ownership mess: `rollup-service` was basically un-owned in practice, so everyone had a partial map and nobody had the whole downstream story. and the `label-name diff` part needs to be explicit because symptom alerts did not point at that at all. from the pages it looked like generic ingest weirdness, not "one label changed and one consumer never got the memo." on May 3 i'd rather write that plainly than over-explain incident mechanics.

bookend_end.content:
Agreed. I’d make the technical-lessons section this literal:

Technical lessons

1. Shard-keeper rollback path: The rollback was easy to make worse under pressure. It looked reversible on paper, but once state had partially moved, it was not a safe or clearly bounded operation.

2. Downstream ownership: rollup-service was effectively unowned in practice. Everyone had part of the downstream map, but nobody owned the complete consumer path.

3. Label-name diff: The label-name change needs to be explicit. Symptom alerts did not identify it; the pages looked like generic ingest weirdness rather than one label changing while a downstream consumer did not receive the change.

This keeps the technical lessons concrete without turning the section into a second incident-mechanics narrative, and it preserves the separate point that the escalation miss was procedural rather than a failure of technical judgment.

# Goal
First-cut controls for the Q4 Cardinality Guardrails work; keep it tied to the September mirror/replay legacy-aggregator wobble without turning validation movement into rollback criteria.

# First-cut matrix

## 1. Label limits
- Failure mode: unbounded or newly introduced label keys/values causing fanout.
- Candidate control: a narrow allowlist or budget per sensitive label family.
- Preflight: flag new high-cardinality labels before a metrics-router or shard-keeper push.

## 2. Alert-source semantics
- Failure mode: responders treating replay/mirror validation movement as live-path rollback evidence.
- Candidate control: dashboard and alert wording that marks live metrics-router traffic separately from replay or mirror validation samples.

## 3. Label-change preflight
- Failure mode: a config or parser change adding labels without checking cardinality behavior.
- Candidate control: a pre-push checklist with sample counts, source label, owner, and rollback/non-rollback semantics.

# Non-goals
- No customer-facing dashboard.
- No general telemetry rewrite.
- No legacy-aggregator retirement claim.
- No claim that the 2% replay sample creates immediate storage savings.
- No Q3 incident framing.

# Monday questions
- What cost examples can Cyrus bring by label family?
- Which preflight checks are service-owned by Alex versus data-platform advisory?
- What would make the first cut too broad?

## Bounded observability example — exception-review outcomes

The accepted production counter uses only these bounded labels:
- `service_pair_class`: `ingest_path`, `routing_path`, `ownership_path`, or `other`
- `exception_class`: `invariant`, `provenance`, `failure_mode`, `ownership`, or `escalation`
- `outcome`: `requested`, `accepted`, or `rejected`

Raw service names, owner email addresses, pull-request identifiers, and reviewer-supplied reasons remain in logs or audit records rather than metric labels. This example creates no centralized review owner: mapped owners retain implementation, operational, release, and rollback responsibility, while boundary review remains limited to the triggered cross-service exception.

# INC-2023-10-30-001 metrics-router canary rollback — lightweight after-action

## Summary
A metrics-router canary for `sha:b41c77a` was rolled back after live-path p99 and dropped writes moved on the canary slice. Replay and mirror validation panels were not the rollback trigger.

## Timeline
- 08:07 ET — Page fired for live metrics-router p99 on canary slice. Alex acknowledged the incident.
- 08:22 ET — Live-path p99 was around 118 ms, error rate was 0.18%, and dropped writes were 0.6% on the canary slice. Alex rolled back the most recent metrics-router deploy.
- 09:05 ET — p99 returned to about 46 ms, error rate returned to roughly 0.02%, and dropped writes returned to zero.

## What changed
The canary appears to have changed the `route_pattern` normalization path so one live handler emitted raw account/widget IDs instead of normalized route patterns. Replay validation still showed normalized route patterns, so replay evidence alone would not have caught the live hot-path value-shape change.

## Why rollback was appropriate
The signal was live-path metrics-router movement: p99 and dropped writes on the canary slice. Replay or mirror validation movement remains investigation evidence, not rollback criteria.

## Follow-ups
1. Keep the code fix small: restore normalized `route_pattern` values for the affected live handler before another canary.
2. Patch the Cardinality Guardrails checklist so live-path label value-shape changes require live canary evidence or a representative live-path fixture, not only replay validation.

## Non-goals
This note is not a broad incident postmortem, not a legacy-aggregator retirement discussion, and not a claim that Cardinality Guardrails is complete.
output.title: INC-2023-10-30-001 metrics-router canary rollback — lightweight after-action

- Participating SDKs reject batches above 8,000 points before transmission.
- The local error tells callers to split the batch before retrying.

- Accepted plus rejected points reconcile to submitted points.

# Deployed status — May 28, 2026

Product Engineering deployed Lantern PR 1089's tenant-scoped published-service alias resolution for Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce on May 28, 2026.

# Resolution rule

Lantern may resolve a historical service identifier only when the tenant-scoped owner map publishes an alias record containing the old identifier, the canonical published service identifier, and an effective interval covering the source event's timestamp. Both the effective interval's start timestamp and end timestamp are inclusive, so a source event timestamp equal to either endpoint is covered.

If no such record exists, the source event timestamp is earlier than the inclusive start timestamp, or the source event timestamp is later than the inclusive end timestamp, Lantern keeps the signals separate and renders ownership as explicit unknown. The UI does not infer a rename from similar names or customer context.

# Harbor Health result

The original Harbor Health `claims-edge` event now resolves to published `claims-ingest` ownership because its source timestamp is covered by the owner map's published alias interval.

# Regression evidence

Across 28 executed fixtures:
- All 12 valid in-interval aliases joined to their canonical published service identifiers.
- Eight out-of-interval aliases remained separate with explicit unknown ownership.
- Eight identifiers with no published alias record remained separate with explicit unknown ownership.

# Affected safety rerun

Alex's affected safety rerun found no cross-tenant resolution, missing provenance, unpublished ownership render, excluded field, adapter call after denial, or loss of read-only enforcement.

# Approved customer-facing wording

Authorized join: `Published service identity resolved from an owner-map alias effective at this source event timestamp.`

No qualifying alias: `Ownership unknown: no published owner-map alias covers this source event timestamp.`

# Unchanged boundary

The deployment applies only to Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce. It adds no heuristic identity inference and does not expand the customer data contract.

## July 3, 2026 — deployed overlap correction

Lantern now evaluates every tenant-scoped owner-map alias whose inclusive effective interval covers the source event timestamp. If all qualifying records identify the same canonical published service, Lantern resolves that identity once. If qualifying records identify two or more distinct canonical services, Lantern keeps the signals separate and renders ownership as explicit unknown regardless of storage order. Both effective-interval endpoints remain inclusive.

Executed regressions show the overlapping Harbor Health `claims-ingest` and `claims-router` records failing closed in both row orders, both inclusive endpoints working, and a single valid match resolving normally. Alex's affected safety rerun found no cross-tenant resolution, missing provenance, unpublished ownership render, excluded field, adapter call after denial, or loss of read-only enforcement.

The correction is live for Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce. Their two-account read-only scope and customer data contract remain unchanged.

# Alex 2026 self-review — evidence draft

Working draft for final portal verification and submission by Friday, November 13, 2026 at 5:00 PM Eastern. The November 12 Lantern result is incorporated. Final portal verification and submission remain pending.

## Submission-form version

### Outcomes and impact — maximum 500 words
In 2026, I turned recurring cross-service ambiguity into explicit invariants, executable evidence, and owner-run decision paths without centralizing routine decisions around me.

The clearest owner-leverage result is metrics-router. Wes became formal primary for implementation, production operations, release and rollback decisions, and owner-led windows. I retained backup coverage and review only for triggered cross-service invariant, provenance, or failure-mode exceptions. On January 20, Wes opened and operated the Mosaic Commerce capacity observation at 17.2 million data points per minute. Every accepted batch reached exactly one terminal result, the full health set remained at baseline, no stop condition fired, and I did not take over the ordinary decision.

Cardinality Guardrails converted label and pipeline risks into reusable controls. I defined cross-service invariants and exception boundaries while mapped owners retained implementation and releases, Nadia retained alert semantics, and Cyrus retained the cost angle. Label-cardinality checks, alert-source classification, and executable parity evidence replaced informal review.

For Lantern, Product Engineering owns implementation; I own the shared contract and failure-mode boundaries. Corrected routing requires my review only for tenant isolation, provenance or authoritative source timestamps, authority duplication or mutation behavior, and customer-path isolation. The reconciled June 16–September 15 evidence covered 2,476 customer sessions, with zero eligible renderer failures and no listed safety violation.

On October 27, that routing found a real exception: insertion order could overwrite either an owner-map or Cardinality Guardrails reference. I blocked the build and internal shadow without taking over Product Engineering’s correction. On November 12, the corrected staff-only build passed 120 fixture runs: all 24 dual-authority cases preserved separate four-part identities and per-record source timestamps in both insertion orders; 12 stale or missing records rendered explicit unknown; eight denied requests made zero adapter calls; and no run crossed tenants, lost required provenance, copied authority values, exposed mutation, or entered either customer path. I closed the triggered contract review, and the build entered bounded internal shadow for Infra and Product Engineering. The integration remains absent from Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce and has not graduated to continuing internal operating use.

### How I worked — maximum 350 words
I made authority, evidence, and escalation boundaries explicit. I separated cross-system contract decisions from implementation and routine operations, leaving those with Product Engineering and mapped service owners. When no named invariant, provenance, authority, or failure-mode exception was triggered, work proceeded without my approval.

I treated metrics-router ownership as a systems outcome rather than a mentoring claim: Wes exercised ordinary authority under accepted controls, while I remained backup and the exception path. For Lantern, I defined the contract boundary while Product Engineering implemented it and Iris retained interpretation and adoption criteria. For Cardinality Guardrails, I defined reusable checks while affected owners retained execution.

I also kept evidence and status precise. I distinguished completed Lantern operating evidence, the October 27 contract block, Product Engineering’s correction, and the bounded November 12 internal-shadow admission without presenting customer exposure or continuing internal operating use as approved.

### Growth focus for 2027 — maximum 200 words
I want to turn more bespoke exception reviews into owner-run executable evidence. This is not delegating people or people management. It means defining coherent authority identity, provenance, failure behavior, stop conditions, and acceptance evidence early enough that mapped owners can run the ordinary path and involve me only when a named cross-system boundary is triggered. I will focus on clearer evidence packages and fewer interpretive review loops while keeping implementation, operations, and people management outside my IC exception role.

## Longer evidence narrative

### Metrics-router owner leverage
Routine authority moved to Wes, while Alex remained formal backup and the named cross-service exception path. The January 20 Mosaic Commerce observation at 17.2 million data points per minute demonstrated that the mapped owner and operating controls worked without Alex taking over an ordinary decision.

Reusable label-cardinality, alert-source, and cross-service parity checks made production review repeatable. Mapped owners retained implementation and releases; Nadia retained alert semantics; Cyrus retained the cost angle.

### Lantern evidence and boundary
The reconciled June 16–September 15 evidence covered 2,476 customer sessions with no listed safety violation. Product Engineering retained implementation, Iris retained interpretation and adoption criteria, and Alex retained only the shared contract and failure-mode boundary.

### November 12 correction
The corrected staff-only build passed the bounded 120-run review and fixed the order-dependent overwrite. Separate owner-map and Cardinality Guardrails references now preserve the required four-part identity and each record’s own source timestamp. The triggered contract review is closed, and the build is in bounded internal shadow for Infra and Product Engineering. # Authority-record time semantics — March 18 brown-bag

## Authoritative source time
`source_timestamp` represents the original authoritative time of the underlying authority record. Later observation, serialization, processing, retry, and navigation times may be recorded as separate metadata, but they must not replace or refresh `source_timestamp`.

## Fail-closed behavior
If a required source timestamp is missing or malformed, downstream navigation fails closed to explicit unknown.

## Multiple authority references
When one card carries multiple authority references, each reference retains its own `source_timestamp`. An envelope time, render time, processing time, or newest retry time must not be substituted for any reference's authoritative source time.

## Unchanged boundaries
This discussion creates no ownership, implementation, release, approval, or customer-authorization change. The internal reference-only integration remains outside the Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce customer paths.

# Q4 incident practice — November 18 scoring sheet

## Scope
A bounded tabletop scoring sheet, not a production runbook. Score observable responder behavior for an accepted metrics-router action across cancellation, caller disconnect, process recovery, and publication.

## Core criteria
1. Durable attempt identity
- Pass: Responders identify the durable acceptance boundary and preserve one attempt identity after acceptance.
- Fail: They create, assume, or accept multiple identities for the same accepted attempt.

2. Terminal accounting
- Pass: Every accepted attempt reaches exactly one terminal result.
- Fail: An accepted attempt has no terminal result or exposes conflicting terminal results.

3. Failure classification
- Pass: Responders distinguish cancellation, caller disconnect, process recovery, and publication using the acceptance boundary.
- Fail: They collapse those cases or treat a pre-acceptance event as evidence about accepted work.

## Wes — responder path
Responders must first determine whether durable acceptance occurred before interpreting cancellation, caller disconnect, process recovery, or publication. After acceptance, they must preserve one durable attempt identity and exactly one terminal result.

## Nadia — postmortem criteria
The postmortem must name the absent system guarantee or control. It must not treat the triggering operator action as the root cause, and it must retain the mapped implementation and rollback owner.

## Final ownership-boundary condition
- Pass: Mapped owners retain implementation and rollback decisions, while the triggered reviewer remains confined to the named failure-mode boundary.
- Fail: The triggered review is treated as implementation, release, or rollback approval.

## Additional operating checks — November 8

### 45-minute secondary boundary
- Pass: When the cause remains unisolated, responders engage the secondary before the 45-minute boundary and make the incident clock visible.
- Fail: Responders wait until or after 45 minutes, or continue without engaging the secondary while the cause remains unisolated.

### Friday staging preparation versus production change
- Pass: Responders identify staging preparation that makes no production state change as staging work and separately identify a Friday-afternoon production deploy as prohibited.
- Fail: Responders classify staging-only preparation as a production deploy, or permit a Friday-afternoon production state change because it was described as preparation.

These checks supplement the accepted cancellation, caller-disconnect, durable-attempt, terminal-result, mapped-owner, and postmortem criteria. This remains a tabletop scoring sheet rather than a production runbook.

## November 18 execution order

- 5 minutes: role and ownership framing.
- 35 minutes: cancellation and caller-disconnect scenario.
- 10 minutes: one targeted rerun if a scoring boundary is missed.
- 10 minutes: debrief and owner follow-up.

Wes teaches the responder path. Nadia owns the postmortem section. Alex maintains only the bounded failure case. This is the exact one-hour tabletop sequence and does not turn the scoring sheet into a production runbook.

## Observed results — November 18

The tabletop is complete. Responders correctly separated durable acceptance from cancellation, caller disconnect, and process recovery; preserved one attempt identity and one terminal result in the exercise; identified Wes as the mapped metrics-router implementation, release, and rollback owner; and distinguished Friday staging preparation from a production change.

The first run engaged the secondary at minute 47 while the cause remained unisolated, missing the required before-45-minute boundary. The targeted rerun engaged the secondary at minute 42 and passed that boundary. Nadia’s debrief named the missing system control rather than the triggering operator action as root cause.

These results are training evidence only. The tabletop did not execute the product implementation and does not close any product defect or replace required executable product evidence.

# Deployed status — May 28, 2026

Product Engineering deployed Lantern PR 1089's tenant-scoped published-service alias resolution for Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce on May 28, 2026.

# Resolution rule

Lantern may resolve a historical service identifier only when the tenant-scoped owner map publishes an alias record containing the old identifier, the canonical published service identifier, and an effective interval covering the source event's timestamp. Both the effective interval's start timestamp and end timestamp are inclusive, so a source event timestamp equal to either endpoint is covered.

If no such record exists, the source event timestamp is earlier than the inclusive start timestamp, or the source event timestamp is later than the inclusive end timestamp, Lantern keeps the signals separate and renders ownership as explicit unknown. The UI does not infer a rename from similar names or customer context.

# Harbor Health result

The original Harbor Health `claims-edge` event now resolves to published `claims-ingest` ownership because its source timestamp is covered by the owner map's published alias interval.

# Regression evidence

Across 28 executed fixtures:
- All 12 valid in-interval aliases joined to their canonical published service identifiers.
- Eight out-of-interval aliases remained separate with explicit unknown ownership.
- Eight identifiers with no published alias record remained separate with explicit unknown ownership.

# Affected safety rerun

Alex's affected safety rerun found no cross-tenant resolution, missing provenance, unpublished ownership render, excluded field, adapter call after denial, or loss of read-only enforcement.

# Approved customer-facing wording

Authorized join: `Published service identity resolved from an owner-map alias effective at this source event timestamp.`

No qualifying alias: `Ownership unknown: no published owner-map alias covers this source event timestamp.`

# Unchanged boundary

The deployment applies only to Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce. It adds no heuristic identity inference and does not expand the customer data contract.

## July 3, 2026 — deployed overlap correction

Lantern now evaluates every tenant-scoped owner-map alias whose inclusive effective interval covers the source event timestamp. If all qualifying records identify the same canonical published service, Lantern resolves that identity once. If qualifying records identify two or more distinct canonical services, Lantern keeps the signals separate and renders ownership as explicit unknown regardless of storage order. Both effective-interval endpoints remain inclusive.

Executed regressions show the overlapping Harbor Health `claims-ingest` and `claims-router` records failing closed in both row orders, both inclusive endpoints working, and a single valid match resolving normally. Alex's affected safety rerun found no cross-tenant resolution, missing provenance, unpublished ownership render, excluded field, adapter call after denial, or loss of read-only enforcement.

The correction is live for Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce. Their two-account read-only scope and customer data contract remain unchanged.
