arguments.title: Metrics-router ownership review — December 5 pre-read
arguments.body:
Purpose

Concise evidence pre-read for the December 5 metrics-router ownership review. This document records the evidence and the questions for review; it does not recommend or imply an outcome in advance.

Evidence

1. First-pass canary decisions and accepted reference

- Wes has made bounded first-pass metrics-router canary decisions through the deploy pipeline, including the August 16 cardinality canary and the November 21 sampling-window cleanup canary.
- In the November 21 canary, a replay-validation panel twitched after the canary slice went live, while live metrics-router p99, live error rate, dropped writes, and rollup-service lag stayed flat. Wes used dashboard source labels to distinguish replay/mirror validation from live-path health, held promotion briefly, rechecked live-path and rollup signals, and proceeded without Alex taking over the decision.
- The accepted canary-response reference covers consistency, route parity, dropped-series, reload, restart, availability, p99, heap, and rollback conditions. The exercised reference also preserves the owner-led-window limits: retired generations must remain at four or fewer; cleanup pauses must remain at or below 100 ms; and the full health set must return to baseline after every push.
- The reference distinguishes a stopped window from recovery. A threshold breach stops the window immediately. Recovery requires preserving the triggering evidence, draining retired generations to one or fewer, confirming p99 and heap at baseline, rerunning the full health set, and obtaining a fresh explicit decision. That decision may authorize at most one distinct, single-file, fully observed recovery push; it does not reopen the prior window. Any subsequent push or later window requires another fresh decision.

2. Owner-led windows and deploy-pipeline operation

- Wes has repeatedly operated within owner-led windows only after the applicable opening decision and within the named service, environment, cohort, baseline, halt triggers, rollback criteria, recovery plan, and decision-owner rules.
- The September owner-led window used the deploy pipeline and staged movement rather than ad hoc or laptop deployment. Alex opened the window; Wes executed the staged movement; the mapped service owners supplied rollup, parity, lease, alert, and related evidence.
- The operating rules preserved the immediate-stop conditions: queue-wait p99 above 400 ms for five consecutive minutes; retryable queue-full responses above 0.5% for five consecutive minutes; any accepted-batch loss; or any departure in consistency, parity, dropped-series, route, shard-keeper lease, rollup, or full-health checks.

3. Tenant-bounded queue operating slice and diagnostics

- Wes maintains the bounded metrics-router operating slice and its diagnostics; this is operational evidence within the existing ownership map, not formal primary ownership.
- The accepted bounded response caps the global queue at 2,048 batches and each tenant at 64 pending batches. Additional work uses the existing retryable backpressure path before acceptance.
- The accepted operator diagnostic does not infer tenant identity from aggregate metrics. It uses a permissioned tenant-bounded snapshot listing up to 20 tenants that hit the 64-pending-batch bound or received a retryable refusal, with an overflow count for additional tenants. In the 200-tenant stress case, 20 listed plus overflow 180 reconciled to all 200 tenants.
- Wes’s signed operator-diagnostics artifact preserved the tenant-list limit, overflow accounting, and reconciliation boundary.

4. September staged rollout

- Eligibility was established by a 90-minute replay at 18.4 million data points per minute, 15% above Mosaic Commerce’s 16.0-million forecast peak: queue-wait p99 was 230 ms, retryable queue-full was 0.07%, no tenant exceeded 64 pending batches, no accepted points were lost, and lease health, rollup parity, route consistency, dropped-series, and full-health checks stayed at baseline.
- The September 24–26 production sequence was bounded: 10% followed by baseline verification, then 50% on September 24; 100% on September 25 only after the prior evidence and full-health baseline; and monitoring only on September 26 with no production push.
- At 50%, queue-wait p99 was 218 ms and retryable queue-full was 0.05%, with no accepted-point loss and baseline health checks. At 100% on September 25, the 14.2-million-data-points-per-minute peak had queue-wait p99 of 240 ms and retryable queue-full of 0.06%; no accepted points were lost, all required checks remained at baseline, and no stop or rollback condition was reached.
- Metrics-router now runs the tenant-bounded queue and retryable-backpressure control in production. The rollout evidence did not change the formal service-owner map.

5. October 6 Mosaic Commerce ramp

- During the announced production ramp, Mosaic Commerce reached 16.0 million data points per minute. At the observed peak, metrics-router queue-wait p99 was 286 ms and retryable queue-full was 0.11%; neither numeric stop threshold was breached for five consecutive minutes.
- No tenant exceeded 64 pending batches; no accepted points were lost; route consistency, dropped-series, shard-keeper lease health, rollup-service parity, and the full health set remained at baseline. Wes independently ran the operating slice and diagnostics while Alex watched the cross-service invariants. No production change or rollback was made, and the tenant-bounded control remained enabled.
- Measurement boundary: the observation recorded accepted points rather than accepted batches. It therefore does not establish whether the accepted-batch loss stop condition was reached. The result is a bounded watch result, not closure of the broader Mosaic scale-response cycle.

6. Accepted-batch diagnostic

- Wes and Nadia supplied the missing executed restart-during-requeue evidence across 25,000 injected crash-and-restart runs, including exits after requeue intent was durably recorded but before the replacement transport attempt was linked.
- Recovery retained the same durable accepted_batch_id, linked every replacement transport attempt before dispatch, and reconciled each accepted batch to exactly one terminal result. Coverage included one and two consecutive requeues. Pre-acceptance refusals stayed outside the accepted-batch population; raw accepted-batch and transport-attempt identities stayed out of metric labels; and the permissioned diagnostic performed reconciliation.
- This closes the restart-during-requeue evidence gap and qualifies the diagnostic for prospective production observation. It does not retroactively establish whether any accepted batch was lost on October 6.

Decision questions for December 5

Routine metrics-router implementation

- What, if any, change in Wes’s authority is appropriate for routine metrics-router implementation within the existing deploy-pipeline and mapped-owner rules?
- What evidence, review, or escalation requirements should remain attached to that authority?

Production operations

- What, if any, change is appropriate for Wes’s bounded operating-slice and diagnostic responsibilities in production?
- Which signals remain first-pass decisions for Wes, and which require escalation or explicit pairing?

Release and rollback decisions

- What, if any, release, staged-movement, rollback, or recovery decisions may Wes make independently within the accepted runbook and deploy-pipeline rules?
- Which conditions require Alex’s explicit decision, a fresh owner-led-window decision, or mapped service-owner involvement?

Authority to open an owner-led window

- Should authority to open an owner-led metrics-router window remain with Alex, or should any narrower authority be assigned?
- If authority changes, what exact scope, evidence, thresholds, stop conditions, recovery sequence, decision owner, and post-window review requirements would define it?

Bounded cross-service exception review

- What, if any, bounded role should Wes have in reviewing exceptions that touch metrics-router and adjacent services while preserving mapped ownership of shard-keeper, rollup-service, and other service-specific decisions?
- What cross-service invariant or failure-mode conditions require Alex’s review, and what evidence is required before an exception can proceed?

Unchanged boundaries pending review

- I remain metrics-router primary and Wes remains backup.
- Shard-keeper remains outside Wes’s solo scope unless I or the Cyrus-team backup explicitly pairs with him.
- The broader Mosaic scale-response cycle remains open.
- No capacity-related production window is authorized.

Outcomes and impact
I improved cross-service reliability by defining explicit invariants and failure boundaries, then turning them into owner-run operating evidence. messages.content:
Cardinality and identifier risks

Raw identifiers and free-form proposal text are poor metric labels because they are effectively unbounded:

- Every new tenant, request, replay source, branch, fixture, proposal, or owner can create another time series.
- Series churn grows storage, ingestion, indexing, and query costs even when traffic volume is unchanged.
- Small wording changes—IDs, timestamps, error details, or punctuation—split what should be one operational signal into many series.
- High-cardinality labels make dashboards and alerts slow, noisy, and difficult to aggregate.
- Raw refusal text may expose account, request, policy, or internal implementation details to telemetry consumers.
- An attacker or malformed input could deliberately amplify series creation by supplying unique values.
- A sampled distinct-count check is useful preflight evidence, but it does not prove that future values will remain bounded.
- A hashed identifier is not automatically safe: `tenant_id_hash` or `replay_source_id` can still have one value per entity and therefore remain effectively unbounded.

The rule should be narrow: do not use effectively unbounded identifiers or raw free-form text as metric labels. Preserve those values for debugging in structured logs, traces, or audit records. Use a small, documented classification enum when aggregate operational visibility requires the dimension.

Draft bounded metric design

Metric name

`proposal_decisions_total`

Purpose

Count proposal decisions and refusal outcomes for operational dashboards and alerts without exposing or indexing raw proposal content, identifiers, or owner records as metric labels.

Metric labels

Use only labels whose value sets are explicitly bounded and stable:

```text
service          = metrics-router | shard-keeper | rollup-service | ...
environment      = production | staging | canary
decision_class   = accepted | refused_policy | refused_shape |
                   refused_authority | refused_dependency | other
source_class     = live | replay | mirror | validation
owner_class      = core | ingest | data_platform |
                   product_surface | unowned_pending
```

The exact enum values should be approved by the service owner and documented with an expected maximum cardinality. No raw IDs, names, URLs, branch names, tenant values, proposal text, or refusal strings belong in these labels.

Example metric

```text
proposal_decisions_total{
  service="metrics-router",
  environment="production",
  decision_class="refused_authority",
  source_class="live",
  owner_class="data_platform"
}
```

If `owner_class` is not needed for a dashboard or alert, omit it. A label should earn its place through a concrete aggregation or filtering need; otherwise it increases the series budget without adding visibility.

Raw diagnostic record

Write the complete details to structured logs or an audit record associated with the metric event:

```json
{
  "event": "proposal_decision",
  "event_version": 1,
  "timestamp": "2027-03-22T09:40:00-04:00",
  "service": "metrics-router",
  "environment": "production",
  "decision_class": "refused_authority",
  "source_class": "live",
  "owner_class": "data_platform",

  "proposal_id": "proposal-raw-id",
  "raw_proposal": {
    "requested_change": "...",
    "refusal_reason": "...",
    "submitted_by": "...",
    "requested_owner": "...",
    "source_reference": "..."
  },

  "owner_record": {
    "owner": "...",
    "owner_source": "...",
    "authority_record_id": "...",
    "decision_owner": "..."
  },

  "correlation_id": "...",
  "audit_record_id": "..."
}
```

The raw proposal and owner details should be access-controlled and retained according to the normal log/audit policy. They should not be copied into metric labels merely because they are useful during investigation.

Operational safeguards

   - Document every allowed value and its meaning.
   - Record the expected maximum number of values for each l…

arguments.title: Alex midyear operating evidence — June 2027
arguments.body:
Alex midyear operating evidence — June 2027

Audience: Hema’s management chain

Purpose and status split

Completed evidence is listed separately from open boundaries below. The completed items close the evidence they name; they do not transfer implementation, release, rollback, customer-interpretation, or ordinary operational authority to Alex. The open items remain explicitly unresolved and must not be read as final intake effectiveness, a frozen Lantern package, or a new authorization decision.

Completed evidence

1. Mosaic 18.0M cycle — owner-preserving closeout

The Mosaic 18.0M capacity-evidence cycle is closed without a queue or configuration change. The closeout preserves the operating model: mapped owners retain implementation and release authority, and the closeout does not create a centralized approval role or transfer ordinary operational decisions to Alex. Wes’s owner-held execution kept readiness aligned with serving eligibility and retained release and rollback ownership; the cycle closed on evidence rather than by reopening production or changing scope.

2. Metrics-router PR 2141 — clean rollout and responder-path teaching

Wes’s PR 2141 rollout was clean and remained owner-held. Wes owns metrics-router implementation, release, and rollback, including the ordinary rollout decisions. The operating follow-through is to turn those decisions into explicit responder-path teaching: Wes teaches the responder path so responders can recognize the relevant signals, follow the mapped escalation route, and understand when rollback remains his decision. Nadia reviews the postmortem section. Alex maintains only cross-service failure cases and reviews named triggered boundaries; Alex is not the routine implementation, release, or rollback approver.

3. Ingest-edge May 24–25 reconciliation — owner-preserving closeout

The May 24–25 ingest-edge reconciliation is complete. Every request accepted during the zone imbalance had exactly one caller-visible terminal result; there was no duplicated or unaccounted accepted work, no leaked queue occupancy, and the empty queues ended at zero. Zone distribution and caller error rate remained at baseline overnight. The service-discovery membership issue was resolved, no owner-map entry changed, and no production window remained open. This closes the reconciliation evidence without changing ingest-edge ownership or admission behavior.

4. Privileged-access recertification — complete

Alex completed the Sphere privileged-access recertification before the May 21, 2027 deadline. The certification recorded that ingest-edge and shard-keeper access remain required for current owner responsibilities and that the stale legacy-aggregator write grant had already been removed. The portal showed the recertification complete, with no remaining access-review task and no service-ownership change.

Open boundaries

1. Corrected exception intake — interim routing observations only

The corrected cross-service exception intake requires each request to name the mapped implementation or release owner, select exactly one boundary class (invariant, provenance, failure_mode, ownership, or escalation), and state the observed failed or at-risk condition. Requests with missing fields return to the mapped owner without entering Alex’s lane; requests that do enter it receive review only of the named boundary, never implementation or release approval. The completed audit identified 13 bounded exceptions and 21 misrouted ordinary-review requests; after the May 12 correction, the first six requests included five that met the bounded-routing requirements and one ordinary release-approval request returned before review. The later full exception-routing sample is not complete. These remain interim routing observations only—not a final claim about intake effectiveness and not a basis for another intake change.

2. Lantern — open, unfrozen April 1–June 15 evidence cycle

The April 1–June 15 Lantern operating-evidence cycle remains open and unfrozen. The authorization is unchanged and limited to the existing two-account scope: Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce; no expansion, renewal, broader-product validation, or new customer authorization is implied. Product Engineering owns Lantern implementation, Iris owns customer interpretation, and Alex maintains only cross-service failure cases and reviews named triggered shared-contract or failure-boundary conditions. The cycle includes the required audit of customer-visible chronology against authoritative source_timestamp values, but it is not complete or final, and no Lantern-completion claim is made.

The seven retry or delayed-processing audit rows missing processing_attempt_id remain open for alternate-key reconciliation. Each row retains a tenant-scoped authority_record_id and a valid authoritative source_timestamp; processing, retry, observation, serialization, and render times cannot substitute for or refresh source_timestamp. The rows are not verified source-ordering rows until the reconciliation is completed.

3. Shard-keeper audit compaction — review remains open

Cyrus’s revised design keeps signed transition envelopes and their original source_timestamp values immutable. Only the derived lookup index is compacted after 30 days, and historical reads rebuild from the retained transition log. Ordinary rebuild fixtures pass, but no executed test yet covers a crash during index replacement or proves that restart cannot expose a partially rebuilt index. The compaction review therefore remains open; it is not a completed production-readiness finding.

Ownership and decision boundary

Mapped owners retain implementation and release authority. Wes owns metrics-router implementation, release, and rollback and teaches the responder path; Nadia reviews the postmortem section; Product Engineering owns Lantern implementation; Iris owns customer interpretation; and Alex maintains only cross-service failure cases and named triggered shared-contract or failure-boundary review. This brief does not claim final intake effectiveness, does not mark the Lantern package frozen or complete, and does not authorize expanded access or continuation.

arguments.body:
Alex midyear operating evidence — June 2027

Audience: Hema’s management chain

Purpose and status split

Completed evidence is listed separately from open boundaries below. The completed items close the evidence they name; they do not transfer implementation, release, rollback, customer-interpretation, or ordinary operational authority to Alex. The open items remain explicitly unresolved and must not be read as final intake effectiveness, a frozen Lantern package, or a new authorization decision.

Completed evidence

1. Mosaic 18.0M cycle — owner-preserving closeout

The Mosaic 18.0M capacity-evidence cycle is closed without a queue or configuration change. The closeout preserves the operating model: mapped owners retain implementation and release authority, and the closeout does not create a centralized approval role or transfer ordinary operational decisions to Alex. Wes’s owner-held execution kept readiness aligned with serving eligibility and retained release and rollback ownership; the cycle closed on evidence rather than by reopening production or changing scope.

2. Metrics-router PR 2141 — clean rollout and responder-path teaching

Wes’s PR 2141 rollout was clean and remained owner-held. Wes owns metrics-router implementation, release, and rollback, including the ordinary rollout decisions. The operating follow-through is to turn those decisions into explicit responder-path teaching: Wes teaches the responder path so responders can recognize the relevant signals, follow the mapped escalation route, and understand when rollback remains his decision. Nadia reviews the postmortem section. Alex maintains only cross-service failure cases and reviews named triggered boundaries; Alex is not the routine implementation, release, or rollback approver.

3. Ingest-edge May 24–25 reconciliation — owner-preserving closeout

The May 24–25 ingest-edge reconciliation is complete. Every request accepted during the zone imbalance had exactly one caller-visible terminal result; there was no duplicated or unaccounted accepted work, no leaked queue occupancy, and the empty queues ended at zero. Zone distribution and caller error rate remained at baseline overnight. The service-discovery membership issue was resolved, no owner-map entry changed, and no production window remained open. This closes the reconciliation evidence without changing ingest-edge ownership or admission behavior.

4. Privileged-access recertification — complete

Alex completed the Sphere privileged-access recertification before the May 21, 2027 deadline. The certification recorded that ingest-edge and shard-keeper access remain required for current owner responsibilities and that the stale legacy-aggregator write grant had already been removed. The portal showed the recertification complete, with no remaining access-review task and no service-ownership change.

Open boundaries

1. Corrected exception intake — interim routing observations only

The corrected cross-service exception intake requires each request to name the mapped implementation or release owner, select exactly one boundary class (invariant, provenance, failure_mode, ownership, or escalation), and state the observed failed or at-risk condition. Requests with missing fields return to the mapped owner without entering Alex’s lane; requests that do enter it receive review only of the named boundary, never implementation or release approval. The completed audit identified 13 bounded exceptions and 21 misrouted ordinary-review requests; after the May 12 correction, the first six requests included five that met the bounded-routing requirements and one ordinary release-approval request returned before review. The later full exception-routing sample is not complete. These remain interim routing observations only—not a final claim about intake effectiveness and not a basis for another intake change.

2. Lantern — open, unfrozen April 1–June 15 evidence cycle

The April 1–June 15 Lantern operating-evidence cycle remains open and unfrozen. The authorization is unchanged and limited to the existing two-account scope: Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce; no expansion, renewal, broader-product validation, or new customer authorization is implied. Product Engineering owns Lantern implementation, Iris owns customer interpretation, and Alex maintains only cross-service failure cases and reviews named triggered shared-contract or failure-boundary conditions. The cycle includes the required audit of customer-visible chronology against authoritative source_timestamp values, but it is not complete or final, and no Lantern-completion claim is made.

The seven retry or delayed-processing audit rows missing processing_attempt_id remain open for alternate-key reconciliation. Each row retains a tenant-scoped authority_record_id and a valid authoritative source_timestamp; processing, retry, observation, serialization, and render times cannot substitute for or refresh source_timestamp. The rows are not verified source-ordering rows until the reconciliation is completed.

3. Shard-keeper audit compaction — review remains open

Cyrus’s revised design keeps signed transition envelopes and their original source_timestamp values immutable. Only the derived lookup index is compacted after 30 days, and historical reads rebuild from the retained transition log. Ordinary rebuild fixtures pass, but no executed test yet covers a crash during index replacement or proves that restart cannot expose a partially rebuilt index. The compaction review therefore remains open; it is not a completed production-readiness finding.

Ownership and decision boundary

Mapped owners retain implementation and release authority. Wes owns metrics-router implementation, release, and rollback and teaches the responder path; Nadia reviews the postmortem section; Product Engineering owns Lantern implementation; Iris owns customer interpretation; and Alex maintains only cross-service failure cases and named triggered shared-contract or failure-boundary review. This brief does not claim final intake effectiveness, does not mark the Lantern package frozen or complete, and does not authorize expanded access or continuation.

messages.content:
Cardinality Guardrails — First-Slice PR/Review Checklist

Scope

Apply this checklist to metrics-router or shard-keeper changes that:

- Add, remove, rename, or repurpose label keys.
- Change label values, parsing, routing, sampling, or fanout behavior.
- Change dashboards or alerts that combine live traffic with replay/mirror validation data.
- Change a label name or contract consumed by rollup-service.

A high-cardinality label is not automatically forbidden. The change may pass when the cardinality is measured, understood, bounded where appropriate, and owned by the affected service.

1. Label-change inventory

[ ] PASS: The PR lists every new, removed, renamed, or behaviorally changed label key.

[ ] PASS: For each changed label, the PR identifies:
    - Source of the label.
    - Expected value shape and approximate distinct count.
    - Whether the label is present on live traffic, replay data, mirror data, or more than one.
    - Owning service and reviewer.

[ ] FAIL: Any label change is implicit in a parser, config, routing, or serialization change and is not called out.

[ ] FAIL: The PR relies on “high cardinality” alone as the reason to reject the change without showing the affected label family, expected fanout, or control rationale.

2. Cardinality preflight

[ ] PASS: The author provides a representative sample or test result showing distinct counts or a defensible estimate for each new or materially changed label.

[ ] PASS: The sample identifies its source and scope, including whether it represents live traffic, replay, mirror, staging, or synthetic data.

[ ] PASS: The PR explains why the observed cardinality is acceptable for the target service.

[ ] PASS: A sensitive label family has an explicit limit, budget, narrow allowlist, or equivalent guard when an unbounded or rapidly expanding value set could create fanout.

[ ] PASS: The control is proportionate to the risk. A bounded high-cardinality label can pass; an unbounded or unexplained label does not.

[ ] FAIL: The change introduces a label whose values can grow with an unbounded identifier space and provides no bound, budget, sampling behavior, or rejection path.

[ ] FAIL: The preflight uses a nonrepresentative sample without documenting the limitation or follow-up control.

[ ] FAIL: The PR claims that a replay or mirror percentage will produce immediate storage savings without measured evidence.

3. Live-versus-validation alert boundary

[ ] PASS: Dashboards, alerts, and review notes distinguish live metrics-router or shard-keeper traffic from replay and mirror validation samples.

[ ] PASS: Alert names, labels, and descriptions make the source classification visible to a responder.

[ ] PASS: The PR states whether each observed movement is:
    - Live-path operational evidence.
    - Replay/mirror validation evidence.
    - Investigation input for future controls.

[ ] PASS: A rollback trigger is based on live-path behavior or another explicitly approved operational signal.

[ ] FAIL: Replay or mirror validation movement alone is presented as evidence that the live path must be rolled back.

[ ] FAIL: A dashboard or alert combines live and validation samples without an unambiguous source label.

[ ] FAIL: The change silently changes the meaning of an existing alert by adding validation data to a live-path signal.

Required review statement:

“Replay/mirror movement is validation and investigation evidence, not a rollback criterion by itself. Rollback requires an affected live-path signal or an explicitly documented operational condition.”

4. Rollup-service parity

Complete this section whenever a label name or label contract crosses from metrics-router or shard-keeper into rollup-service or another downstream consumer.

[ ] PASS: The PR identifies the downstream consumer and states whether the label key and value semantics are expected to remain compatible.

[ ] PASS: The author or service owner confirms that rollup-service recognizes the same labe…

# Oversized-batch design and staged enablement

## Selected permanent behavior
- Participating SDKs reject batches above 8,000 points before transmission.
- The local error tells callers to split the batch before retrying.
- Ingest-edge retains a deterministic backstop for older or nonconforming clients.
- The backstop returns HTTP 413, accepts zero points, reports rejected points equal to the submitted count, and uses the machine-readable `oversized_batch` reason.
- Clients must not retry an unchanged oversized request.

## Evidence behind the decision
- Current SDK clients rejected oversized attempts locally without network transmission.
- Split compliant requests reconciled accepted-point accounting.
- The older client received the deterministic ingest-edge response, made no unchanged retry, and succeeded after splitting.
- The corrected SDK error text names the 8,000-point maximum and the split-before-retry action.

## Enablement window
Stage enablement through January 28, with participating SDK prevention first and ingest-edge retained as the server-side backstop.

## Verification and stop checks
- No unchanged retry after local rejection or HTTP 413.
- Accepted plus rejected points reconcile to submitted points.
- Split requests do not duplicate or lose points.
- Compliant traffic remains at baseline error and latency levels.

The design is selected; this document does not claim staged enablement is complete.

# Deployed status — May 28, 2026

Product Engineering deployed Lantern PR 1089's tenant-scoped published-service alias resolution for Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce on May 28, 2026.

# Resolution rule

Lantern may resolve a historical service identifier only when the tenant-scoped owner map publishes an alias record containing the old identifier, the canonical published service identifier, and an effective interval covering the source event's timestamp. Both the effective interval's start timestamp and end timestamp are inclusive, so a source event timestamp equal to either endpoint is covered.

If no such record exists, the source event timestamp is earlier than the inclusive start timestamp, or the source event timestamp is later than the inclusive end timestamp, Lantern keeps the signals separate and renders ownership as explicit unknown. The UI does not infer a rename from similar names or customer context.

# Harbor Health result

The original Harbor Health `claims-edge` event now resolves to published `claims-ingest` ownership because its source timestamp is covered by the owner map's published alias interval.

# Regression evidence

Across 28 executed fixtures:
- All 12 valid in-interval aliases joined to their canonical published service identifiers.
- Eight out-of-interval aliases remained separate with explicit unknown ownership.
- Eight identifiers with no published alias record remained separate with explicit unknown ownership.

# Affected safety rerun

Alex's affected safety rerun found no cross-tenant resolution, missing provenance, unpublished ownership render, excluded field, adapter call after denial, or loss of read-only enforcement.

# Approved customer-facing wording

Authorized join: `Published service identity resolved from an owner-map alias effective at this source event timestamp.`

No qualifying alias: `Ownership unknown: no published owner-map alias covers this source event timestamp.`

# Unchanged boundary

# Oversized-batch design and staged enablement

## Selected permanent behavior
- Participating SDKs reject batches above 8,000 points before transmission.
- The local error tells callers to split the batch before retrying.
- Ingest-edge retains a deterministic backstop for older or nonconforming clients.
- The backstop returns HTTP 413, accepts zero points, reports rejected points equal to the submitted count, and uses the machine-readable `oversized_batch` reason.
- Clients must not retry an unchanged oversized request.

## Evidence behind the decision
- Current SDK clients rejected oversized attempts locally without network transmission.
- Split compliant requests reconciled accepted-point accounting.
- The older client received the deterministic ingest-edge response, made no unchanged retry, and succeeded after splitting.
- The corrected SDK error text names the 8,000-point maximum and the split-before-retry action.

## Enablement window
Stage enablement through January 28, with participating SDK prevention first and ingest-edge retained as the server-side backstop.

## Verification and stop checks
- No unchanged retry after local rejection or HTTP 413.
- Accepted plus rejected points reconcile to submitted points.
- Split requests do not duplicate or lose points.
- Compliant traffic remains at baseline error and latency levels.

The design is selected; this document does not claim staged enablement is complete.

# Metrics-router canary-response walkthrough — facilitator sheet

> **PROMINENT RECOVERY CALLOUT:** After a stopped window recovers, a fresh decision permits exactly one fully observed push. It does not reopen the whole window. A later multi-push window requires another separate fresh opening decision after that recovery push returns the full health set to baseline.

## 1. Opening decision versus operator actions
- Every owner-led configuration window requires a fresh opening decision from Alex.
- After the window opens, mapped operators may make single-file pushes without another approval before every safe push.

## 2. In-window limits
- Retired generations must remain at four or fewer.
- Cleanup pauses must remain at or below 100 milliseconds.
- The full health set must return to baseline after every push before another push proceeds.

## 3. Stop and rollback conditions
- Crossing either the retired-generation or cleanup-pause threshold stops the window immediately.
- Active-generation inconsistency, route-parity failure, dropped series, reload failure, or restart remains a rollback condition.

## 4. Correct recovery sequence
1. Recover and re-establish the full health set.

# Deployed status — May 28, 2026

Product Engineering deployed Lantern PR 1089's tenant-scoped published-service alias resolution for Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce on May 28, 2026.

# Resolution rule

Lantern may resolve a historical service identifier only when the tenant-scoped owner map publishes an alias record containing the old identifier, the canonical published service identifier, and an effective interval covering the source event's timestamp. Both the effective interval's start timestamp and end timestamp are inclusive, so a source event timestamp equal to either endpoint is covered.

If no such record exists, the source event timestamp is earlier than the inclusive start timestamp, or the source event timestamp is later than the inclusive end timestamp, Lantern keeps the signals separate and renders ownership as explicit unknown. The UI does not infer a rename from similar names or customer context.

# Harbor Health result

The original Harbor Health `claims-edge` event now resolves to published `claims-ingest` ownership because its source timestamp is covered by the owner map's published alias interval.

# Regression evidence

Across 28 executed fixtures:
- All 12 valid in-interval aliases joined to their canonical published service identifiers.
- Eight out-of-interval aliases remained separate with explicit unknown ownership.
- Eight identifiers with no published alias record remained separate with explicit unknown ownership.

# Affected safety rerun

Alex's affected safety rerun found no cross-tenant resolution, missing provenance, unpublished ownership render, excluded field, adapter call after denial, or loss of read-only enforcement.

# Approved customer-facing wording

Authorized join: `Published service identity resolved from an owner-map alias effective at this source event timestamp.`

No qualifying alias: `Ownership unknown: no published owner-map alias covers this source event timestamp.`

# Unchanged boundary

The deployment applies only to Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce. It adds no heuristic identity inference and does not expand the customer data contract.

## July 3, 2026 — deployed overlap correction

Lantern now evaluates every tenant-scoped owner-map alias whose inclusive effective interval covers the source event timestamp. If all qualifying records identify the same canonical published service, Lantern resolves that identity once. If qualifying records identify two or more distinct canonical services, Lantern keeps the signals separate and renders ownership as explicit unknown regardless of storage order. Both effective-interval endpoints remain inclusive.

Executed regressions show the overlapping Harbor Health `claims-ingest` and `claims-router` records failing closed in both row orders, both inclusive endpoints working, and a single valid match resolving normally. Alex's affected safety rerun found no cross-tenant resolution, missing provenance, unpublished ownership render, excluded field, adapter call after denial, or loss of read-only enforcement.

The correction is live for Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce. Their two-account read-only scope and customer data contract remain unchanged.

# Q4 incident practice — November 18 scoring sheet

## Scope
A bounded tabletop scoring sheet, not a production runbook. Score observable responder behavior for an accepted metrics-router action across cancellation, caller disconnect, process recovery, and publication.

## Core criteria
1. Durable attempt identity
- Pass: Responders identify the durable acceptance boundary and preserve one attempt identity after acceptance.
- Fail: They create, assume, or accept multiple identities for the same accepted attempt.

2. Terminal accounting
- Pass: Every accepted attempt reaches exactly one terminal result.
- Fail: An accepted attempt has no terminal result or exposes conflicting terminal results.

3. Failure classification
- Pass: Responders distinguish cancellation, caller disconnect, process recovery, and publication using the acceptance boundary.
- Fail: They collapse those cases or treat a pre-acceptance event as evidence about accepted work.

## Wes — responder path
Responders must first determine whether durable acceptance occurred before interpreting cancellation, caller disconnect, process recovery, or publication. After acceptance, they must preserve one durable attempt identity and exactly one terminal result.

## Nadia — postmortem criteria
The postmortem must name the absent system guarantee or control. It must not treat the triggering operator action as the root cause, and it must retain the mapped implementation and rollback owner.

## Final ownership-boundary condition
- Pass: Mapped owners retain implementation and rollback decisions, while the triggered reviewer remains confined to the named failure-mode boundary.
- Fail: The triggered review is treated as implementation, release, or rollback approval.

## Additional operating checks — November 8

### 45-minute secondary boundary
- Pass: When the cause remains unisolated, responders engage the secondary before the 45-minute boundary and make the incident clock visible.
- Fail: Responders wait until or after 45 minutes, or continue without engaging the secondary while the cause remains unisolated.

# Oversized-batch design and staged enablement

## Selected permanent behavior
- Participating SDKs reject batches above 8,000 points before transmission.
- The local error tells callers to split the batch before retrying.
- Ingest-edge retains a deterministic backstop for older or nonconforming clients.
- The backstop returns HTTP 413, accepts zero points, reports rejected points equal to the submitted count, and uses the machine-readable `oversized_batch` reason.
- Clients must not retry an unchanged oversized request.

- Current SDK clients rejected oversized attempts locally without network transmission.
- Split compliant requests reconciled accepted-point accounting.
- The older client received the deterministic ingest-edge response, made no unchanged retry, and succeeded after splitting.

Stage enablement through January 28, with participating SDK prevention first and ingest-edge retained as the server-side backstop.

- No unchanged retry after local rejection or HTTP 413.
- Accepted plus rejected points reconcile to submitted points.
- Split requests do not duplicate or lose points.
- Compliant traffic remains at baseline error and latency levels.

# Deployed status — May 28, 2026

Product Engineering deployed Lantern PR 1089's tenant-scoped published-service alias resolution for Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce on May 28, 2026.

# Resolution rule

Lantern may resolve a historical service identifier only when the tenant-scoped owner map publishes an alias record containing the old identifier, the canonical published service identifier, and an effective interval covering the source event's timestamp. Both the effective interval's start timestamp and end timestamp are inclusive, so a source event timestamp equal to either endpoint is covered.

If no such record exists, the source event timestamp is earlier than the inclusive start timestamp, or the source event timestamp is later than the inclusive end timestamp, Lantern keeps the signals separate and renders ownership as explicit unknown. The UI does not infer a rename from similar names or customer context.

# Harbor Health result

The original Harbor Health `claims-edge` event now resolves to published `claims-ingest` ownership because its source timestamp is covered by the owner map's published alias interval.

# Regression evidence

Across 28 executed fixtures:
- All 12 valid in-interval aliases joined to their canonical published service identifiers.
- Eight out-of-interval aliases remained separate with explicit unknown ownership.
- Eight identifiers with no published alias record remained separate with explicit unknown ownership.

Alex's affected safety rerun found no cross-tenant resolution, missing provenance, unpublished ownership render, excluded field, adapter call after denial, or loss of read-only enforcement.

Authorized join: `Published service identity resolved from an owner-map alias effective at this source event timestamp.`

# Authority-record time semantics — March 18 brown-bag

## Authoritative source time
`source_timestamp` represents the original authoritative time of the underlying authority record. Later observation, serialization, processing, retry, and navigation times may be recorded as separate metadata, but they must not replace or refresh `source_timestamp`.

## Fail-closed behavior
If a required source timestamp is missing or malformed, downstream navigation fails closed to explicit unknown.

## Multiple authority references
When one card carries multiple authority references, each reference retains its own `source_timestamp`. An envelope time, render time, processing time, or newest retry time must not be substituted for any reference's authoritative source time.

## Unchanged boundaries
This discussion creates no ownership, implementation, release, approval, or customer-authorization change. The internal reference-only integration remains outside the Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce customer paths.

A reassessment was completed at 16:55, and the entry documenting it was made at 17:40.

“Late entry entered at 17:40 for a reassessment performed at 16:55. This entry records the findings from the 16:55 reassessment and does not alter the earlier record.”

# Q4 incident practice — November 18 scoring sheet

## Scope
A bounded tabletop scoring sheet, not a production runbook. Score observable responder behavior for an accepted metrics-router action across cancellation, caller disconnect, process recovery, and publication.

## Core criteria
1. Durable attempt identity
- Pass: Responders identify the durable acceptance boundary and preserve one attempt identity after acceptance.
- Fail: They create, assume, or accept multiple identities for the same accepted attempt.

2. Terminal accounting
- Pass: Every accepted attempt reaches exactly one terminal result.
- Fail: An accepted attempt has no terminal result or exposes conflicting terminal results.

3. Failure classification
- Pass: Responders distinguish cancellation, caller disconnect, process recovery, and publication using the acceptance boundary.
- Fail: They collapse those cases or treat a pre-acceptance event as evidence about accepted work.

## Wes — responder path
Responders must first determine whether durable acceptance occurred before interpreting cancellation, caller disconnect, process recovery, or publication. After acceptance, they must preserve one durable attempt identity and exactly one terminal result.

## Nadia — postmortem criteria
The postmortem must name the absent system guarantee or control. It must not treat the triggering operator action as the root cause, and it must retain the mapped implementation and rollback owner.

## Final ownership-boundary condition

- Fail: The triggered review is treated as implementation, release, or rollback approval.

## Selected permanent behavior
- Participating SDKs reject batches above 8,000 points before transmission.
- The local error tells callers to split the batch before retrying.

- Accepted plus rejected points reconcile to submitted points.

# Deployed status — May 28, 2026

Product Engineering deployed Lantern PR 1089's tenant-scoped published-service alias resolution for Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce on May 28, 2026.

# Resolution rule

Lantern may resolve a historical service identifier only when the tenant-scoped owner map publishes an alias record containing the old identifier, the canonical published service identifier, and an effective interval covering the source event's timestamp. Both the effective interval's start timestamp and end timestamp are inclusive, so a source event timestamp equal to either endpoint is covered.

If no such record exists, the source event timestamp is earlier than the inclusive start timestamp, or the source event timestamp is later than the inclusive end timestamp, Lantern keeps the signals separate and renders ownership as explicit unknown. The UI does not infer a rename from similar names or customer context.

# Harbor Health result

The original Harbor Health `claims-edge` event now resolves to published `claims-ingest` ownership because its source timestamp is covered by the owner map's published alias interval.

# Regression evidence

Across 28 executed fixtures:
- All 12 valid in-interval aliases joined to their canonical published service identifiers.
- Eight out-of-interval aliases remained separate with explicit unknown ownership.
- Eight identifiers with no published alias record remained separate with explicit unknown ownership.

Alex's affected safety rerun found no cross-tenant resolution, missing provenance, unpublished ownership render, excluded field, adapter call after denial, or loss of read-only enforcement.

Authorized join: `Published service identity resolved from an owner-map alias effective at this source event timestamp.`

The deployment applies only to Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce. It adds no heuristic identity inference and does not expand the customer data contract.

Lantern now evaluates every tenant-scoped owner-map alias whose inclusive effective interval covers the source event timestamp. `source_timestamp` represents the original authoritative time of the underlying authority record. Later observation, serialization, processing, retry, and navigation times may be recorded as separate metadata, but they must not replace or refresh `source_timestamp`.

If a required source timestamp is missing or malformed, downstream navigation fails closed to explicit unknown.

When one card carries multiple authority references, each reference retains its own `source_timestamp`. An envelope time, render time, processing time, or newest retry time must not be substituted for any reference's authoritative source time.

# Q4 incident practice — November 18 scoring sheet

## Scope
A bounded tabletop scoring sheet, not a production runbook. Score observable responder behavior for an accepted metrics-router action across cancellation, caller disconnect, process recovery, and publication.

## Core criteria
1. Durable attempt identity
- Pass: Responders identify the durable acceptance boundary and preserve one attempt identity after acceptance.
- Fail: They create, assume, or accept multiple identities for the same accepted attempt.

2. Terminal accounting
- Pass: Every accepted attempt reaches exactly one terminal result.
- Fail: An accepted attempt has no terminal result or exposes conflicting terminal results.

3. Failure classification
- Pass: Responders distinguish cancellation, caller disconnect, process recovery, and publication using the acceptance boundary.
- Fail: They collapse those cases or treat a pre-acceptance event as evidence about accepted work.

## Wes — responder path
Responders must first determine whether durable acceptance occurred before interpreting cancellation, caller disconnect, process recovery, or publication. After acceptance, they must preserve one durable attempt identity and exactly one terminal result.

## Nadia — postmortem criteria
The postmortem must name the absent system guarantee or control. It must not treat the triggering operator action as the root cause, and it must retain the mapped implementation and rollback owner.

## Final ownership-boundary condition
- Pass: Mapped owners retain implementation and rollback decisions, while the triggered reviewer remains confined to the named failure-mode boundary.
- Fail: The triggered review is treated as implementation, release, or rollback approval.

### 45-minute secondary boundary
- Pass: When the cause remains unisolated, responders engage the secondary before the 45-minute boundary and make the incident clock visible.
- Fail: Responders wait until or after 45 minutes, or continue without engaging the secondary while the cause remains unisolated.

### Friday staging preparation versus production change
- Pass: Responders identify staging preparation that makes no production state change as staging work and separately identify a Friday-afternoon production deploy as prohibited.
- Fail: Responders classify staging-only preparation as a production deploy, or permit a Friday-afternoon production state change because it was described as preparation.

These checks supplement the accepted cancellation, caller-disconnect, durable-attempt, terminal-result, mapped-owner, and postmortem criteria. This remains a tabletop scoring sheet rather than a production runbook.

- 5 minutes: role and ownership framing.
- 35 minutes: cancellation and caller-disconnect scenario.
- 10 minutes: one targeted rerun if a scoring boundary is missed.
- 10 minutes: debrief and owner follow-up.

tests.request: Create a short mentoring handout comparing the practical scheduling tradeoffs of chief-resident, hospitalist, and QI/research bridge paths without recommending one.

input.body:
Practical Scheduling Tradeoffs

This handout compares schedule shape—not prestige, fit, or career value. Actual arrangements vary by institution and should be confirmed with sample schedules and written expectations.

Chief resident
- Nights and weekends may cluster around hospital need, even when teaching or administrative time is formally protected.
- Service coverage and urgent operational work can interrupt planned blocks.
- Predictability depends heavily on how the program handles coverage changes and protects recovery after intense stretches.

Hospitalist
- A 7-on/7-off pattern can be predictable on paper and may create clearly defined work blocks.
- The “off” block may be partly consumed by recovery, errands, charting, education, or extra service.
- Important details include personal night coverage, backup or late-day responsibilities, weekend frequency, and advance notice when assignments change.

QI/research bridge
- May involve fewer nights and weekends than service-heavy paths.
- The schedule is workable only if project time is genuinely protected by a named sponsor and clinic/service spillover is limited.
- Before committing, clarify the weekly template, evening-clinic frequency, clinic load, who can override protected time, stipend and benefits, and which terms are guaranteed in writing versus negotiated later.

Questions to compare across paths
- What does a typical week and month look like, including nights, weekends, clinic, administrative work, and recovery time?
- Which parts are fixed before the year starts, and what commonly disrupts them?
- How often do weekend or night assignments cluster, and how much notice is provided?
- What protections, compensation, and benefits are documented before commitment?

The goal is to make the schedule reality visible enough for an informed comparison; this handout does not rank or recommend a path.

tests.request: Create a short document correcting a note that attributes the April 18, 2023 outage solely to shard-keeper. State what changed in shard-keeper, what failed to change downstream, and how that affected the alerts.

input.body:
The April 18, 2023 outage was not caused by shard-keeper alone.

What changed in shard-keeper: the production config push renamed the emitted label from `storage_region` to `region`.

What failed downstream: `rollup-service`, the downstream consumer, was not updated to consume the new label and continued expecting the old name. The shard-keeper-side change therefore broke cross-service label parity.

Effect on alerts: the resulting symptoms surfaced as generic ingest/metrics weirdness. The alerts did not identify the label-name mismatch or clearly show that one consumer had not been updated, delaying diagnosis. The incident also exposed that the shard-keeper rollback path became unsafe once state had partially moved and that rollup-service ownership was unclear in practice.

input.body:
Request changes. This grace-period implementation contradicts the established production lease-handoff behavior: on lease-loss notification, the former holder's serving gate must close before any subsequent routing response. The poll is only a backup detector, not the mechanism that permits the old holder to serve until a successor is observed. With `canServe()` accepting `now < graceUntil`, this PR explicitly allows the old holder to answer while the successor may already be serving, and its test asserts that both holders can return successful responses. That violates the production invariant of exactly one serving holder and can produce stale routing responses.

Please change the handoff ordering to: lease-loss notification atomically closes/fences the old serving gate; no later old-holder routing response may be emitted (including the authorization-to-response race); only then may the replacement acquire/serve. Retain polling solely as a backup detector. Add focused evidence/tests for delayed old-holder responses after lease loss/gate closure, the revoke-after-read-authorization-before-response barrier, repeated/delayed-notification failover with exactly one serving holder, monotonic lease epochs, and explicit stale-response rejection diagnostics.

For production/runbook verification, provide the synthetic-revocation results showing exactly one serving holder throughout, gate-close latency and proof gate closure preceded the next routing response, zero stale responses/reads, replacement acquisition time, request p99 and error movement returning to baseline, and zero restarts. The existing full-production revocations showed exactly those properties: one holder, old gate closed before another routing response, no stale reads, brief latency/error movement back to baseline, and no restarts. Do not treat process availability or a grace interval as sufficient evidence; update implementation/tests and attach these handoff and production checks.

tests.request: Create a short claim-preparation note for a January 1, 2028 South Slope water-backup incident involving about $2,600 of damaged household property and possibly two hotel nights, using the active policy terms without promising coverage.

input.body:
Incident: On January 1, 2028, a water-backup incident at the South Slope residence damaged approximately $2,600 of household property. Two hotel nights may also be necessary; retain itemized lodging receipts and document why the apartment was not reasonably usable, if applicable.

Policy reference: The active renters policy runs through January 5, 2028 and lists a $500 deductible, $40,000 replacement-cost personal-property limit, $12,000 loss-of-use limit, and water-backup endorsement. There are no separate bicycle or electronics sublimits. These terms do not guarantee coverage; the claim remains subject to the full policy, exclusions, conditions, causation findings, limits, and the insurer’s coverage determination.

Before filing: Photograph/video the source, affected areas, and each damaged item; prevent further damage if safe; keep damaged property for inspection unless the insurer authorizes disposal; make an itemized inventory with purchase dates, replacement estimates, and receipts or other proof of ownership; obtain any plumber, remediation, management, and incident reports; and keep all hotel and related expense receipts.

Claim request: Notify the insurer promptly and ask for a claim number, inspection instructions, and a written coverage determination for both the personal-property loss and any reasonable hotel expense. Report the estimated property loss as about $2,600 before the $500 deductible, without treating that estimate or the possible two hotel nights as an admission that either portion is covered.
